items.title: Sécurité des bâtiments : les maires et les ordres professionnels scellent un partenariat
items.summary: © DR Face à la recrudescence des effondrements d'immeubles, les Communes et Villes Unies du Cameroun (CVUC), l'Ordre National des Architectes du Cameroun (ONAC) et l'Ordre National des Ingénieurs de Génie Civil (ONIGC) ont signé ce mercredi 03 septembre 2026 une convention-cadre tripartite historique. Objectif : verrouiller le suivi des chantiers privés après la délivrance du permis de construire.
items.body: © DR Face à la recrudescence des effondrements d'immeubles, les Communes et Villes Unies du Cameroun (CVUC), l'Ordre National des Architectes du Cameroun (ONAC) et l'Ordre National des Ingénieurs de Génie Civil (ONIGC) ont signé ce mercredi 03 septembre 2026 une convention-cadre tripartite historique. Objectif : verrouiller le suivi des chantiers privés après la délivrance du permis de construire. C'est une réponse directe à une crise qui endeuille le Cameroun. Les CVUC, l'ONAC et l'ONIGC ont décidé de siffler la fin du désordre dans le secteur du BTP. Réunies le 03 septembre, les trois parties ont paraphé une convention qui change la donne. Fini le permis de construire délivré puis oublié. Désormais, le dispositif impose une maîtrise d'œuvre conjointe associant obligatoirement architecte et ingénieur sur les chantiers privés. Le texte prévoit des garde-fous concrets : instauration d'un carnet de suivi de chantier, obligation de points d'arrêt aux étapes critiques des travaux pour validation, et mécanisme de paiement progressif des honoraires des professionnels pour éviter les abandons. L'ambition politique est claire : prévenir les malfaçons, stopper les modifications anarchiques des plans approuvés et surtout, redonner aux mairies leur pouvoir de contrôle administratif, souvent contourné. Pour ne pas brusquer le système, une phase pilote sera lancée dans des communes volontaires, avec deux innovations majeures : la digitalisation du carnet de suivi et la formation des agents municipaux. À travers cet accord, les collectivités et les ordres professionnels envoient un message fort : la sécurité des populations prime sur les économies de bout de chandelle. Cet article Sécurité des bâtiments : les maires et les ordres professionnels scellent un partenariat est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Libya arrests five over drone attacks on oil and electricity facilities
items.summary: Libya’s internationally recognised Government of National Unity announced on Sunday that it had dismantled an organised sabotage cell allegedly responsible for suicide drone attacks on oil and electricity facilities in Tripoli and Zawiya. Five Libyan and foreign nationals were arrested during an operation conducted by the Ministry of Defense, according to a statement published on […]
items.body:
Libya’s internationally recognised Government of National Unity announced on Sunday that it had dismantled an organised sabotage cell allegedly responsible for suicide drone attacks on oil and electricity facilities in Tripoli and Zawiya.

Five Libyan and foreign nationals were arrested during an operation conducted by the Ministry of Defense, according to a statement published on the government’s “Hokomitna” platform.

Authorities said the operation also foiled planned attacks on a power station south of Tripoli, other critical facilities and political, security and military leaders.

Investigations are continuing to identify other suspects and those accused of planning, financing or supporting the operations. The government said further details would be released after preliminary investigations were completed. The arrests followed weeks of attacks and sabotage against energy infrastructure in western Libya, which placed additional pressure on electricity supplies and public services during the peak summer period.

items.title: Heavy Gunfire Sparks Fear of Renewed Fighting Near CAR’s Capital
items.summary: The renewed fighting reveals the fragile security situation in CAR, where peace agreements signed in recent years have repeatedly faltered, and where the government continues to struggle to assert authority beyond the capital. The post Heavy Gunfire Sparks Fear of Renewed Fighting Near CAR’s Capital appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Intense fighting involving heavy and light weapons is taking place in the PK40-45 area along the Boali road, which leads to Bangui, the capital of the Central African Republic (CAR). Traffic in and out of the capital via this road has been halted, preventing any vehicles from entering or leaving the town. Local sources in the CAR capital say they have yet to determine the forces involved in the ongoing chaos and exchange of fire. “At this stage, the exact circumstances leading to this exchange of gunfire are not known. No human and material casualty figures are available right now,” a government source who asked for anonymity because he is not authorised to speak on behalf of the government told HumAngle in Bangui. Diplomatic sources suggested that the exchange of gunfire happened between the CAR national army and some of the rebel groups operating in the country. There are currently no physical indications that the authorities in Bangui are preparing to send reinforcements to Boali. The heavy exchange of gunfire near the town of Boali comes amid an ongoing conflict in the country. When a coalition of rebel groups known as the Séléka overthrew President François Bozizé in 2013, CAR was thrown into a cycle of violence between different armed groups, government forces, and international peacekeepers. Despite the deployment of United Nations peacekeepers and bilateral support from allies such as Russia and Rwanda, a huge part of the country is still being controlled by armed rebel groups. The deadly groups often exploit CAR’s weak state institutions, porous borders, and lucrative natural resources, including diamonds and gold, to sustain their operations. The town of Boali strategically lies on the main road linking Bangui to the country’s northern and western regions. Vital for trade, supply routes, and military logistics, this corridor is contested by armed groups and state forces. Past clashes in this area have disrupted humanitarian access and heightened insecurity for civilians, many of whom already face displacement and food shortages. The renewed fighting reveals the fragile security situation in CAR, where peace agreements signed in recent years have repeatedly faltered, and where the government continues to struggle to assert authority beyond the capital. The post Heavy Gunfire Sparks Fear of Renewed Fighting Near CAR’s Capital appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: RSF releases four journalists and lawyer after months in detention in North Darfur
items.summary: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have released four female journalists and a lawyer in Nyala,... The post RSF releases four journalists and lawyer after months in detention in North Darfur appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have released four female journalists and a lawyer in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, after holding them for varying periods of time. Sources tell Radio Dabanga that the journalists, Dr Manahil Mustafa, Ishraqa Abdelrahman, Mawahib Ibrahim, and Zahra Mohamed El Hassan, were released alongside the lawyer, Magda Hassan Ali, after about six months in detention. The journalists and lawyer were arrested after taking part in a workshop held in February that discussed women’s issues and rights. Meanwhile, the family of El Hadi Abdelrahman, the former director general of the Ministry of Education, tells Radio Dabanga that the Rapid Support Forces have also released him after he spent more than a year and a half in Dagris prison in South Darfur. This report follows coverage by Radio Dabanga last week that the Sudanese Journalists’ Syndicate says five of its members remain victims of enforced disappearance, with their fate and whereabouts still unknown. It describes this as a serious violation of their basic rights, international law, and their right to life and personal safety. In a statement, the syndicate calls for the immediate disclosure of the journalists’ fate and whereabouts, and for a serious, independent investigation into the circumstances of their disappearance. Note: This report has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. items.title: Former speaker Kumba urges armed groups to lay down guns
items.summary: Former parliament speaker Jemma Nunu Kumba has called on churches, communities and the government to The post Former speaker Kumba urges armed groups to lay down guns appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: Former parliament speaker Jemma Nunu Kumba has called on churches, communities and the government to work together to persuade armed opposition groups in Western Equatoria state to lay down their weapons and return home. Kumba made the appeal on Sunday during morning prayers at St Mary Church in Yambio, urging communities to take greater responsibility for restoring peace in the state. She said the Zande and Balanda communities had no fundamental differences and blamed continued insecurity largely on the involvement of some members of the communities in armed groups. “The Zande and Balanda have no problem. The problem is our sons and daughters who are still in the bush,” Kumba said. She called for continued dialogue with armed groups and said churches could play a key role in reaching out to opposition fighters and supporting reconciliation efforts. Kumba cited the Inter-Church Interface Group, which she said had previously helped persuade some former members of the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-In Opposition (SPLM-IO) to leave the bush and return to their communities. “Anyone is welcome to put down the gun and come home to join his brothers and sisters to develop our state and our country,” she said. Kumba also appealed to former Western Equatoria governor Alfred Futuyo Karaba to return home with those still associated with him, describing him as a “son of the state.” She said President Salva Kiir Mayardit had granted an amnesty to people carrying guns and urged armed groups to take advantage of the offer by laying down their weapons and returning home. Those who have returned are being integrated into government institutions, including the national army, she said. Kumba also expressed concern about insecurity along the road linking Western Equatoria with the capital, Juba, saying civilians continue to face attacks and killings allegedly carried out by armed groups and criminal elements. “We are brothers and sisters. There is nobody coming from outside now to fight us here. It is us alone,” she said. She said lasting peace would enable children to attend school, farmers to cultivate their land, businesses to operate and people to travel without fear. Kumba said she would work with churches and the government to support efforts to restore lasting peace in Western Equatoria. “So, this is what I can tell you as your mother. We will join hands together with the church and the government to make sure that peace is restored in our state,” she said. Kumba’s appeal follows a similar call by Western Equatoria Governor Badagbu Daniel Rimbasa on Aug. 24 for armed groups operating around Duma, Mapuse, Bandala and Sue to end hostilities, return to their communities and participate in dialogue and peaceful integration. Rimbasa also called for an end to road ambushes and urged parents, relatives and community leaders to encourage young people involved in armed activities to return home. “We are tired of war. We cannot continue destabilizing our own area,” Rimbasa said. The post Former speaker Kumba urges armed groups to lay down guns appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.body: © (Archives) Le président national du Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun s'adresse aux élèves, aux parents, aux enseignants au moment où l'année scolaire 2026/ 2027 commence. Encouragements, appel à la détermination, à la vigilance, à la protection et au meilleur encadrement des enfants sont des mots clés du message que Maurice Kamto adresse à la communauté éducative ce 07 septembre. Aux millions d'élèves attendus dans des établissements scolaires, l'homme politique souhaite santé, enthousiasme, détermination, et réussite. Il voit en ces derniers « l'espoir des transformations multiformes à venir » du Cameroun et de l'Afrique. Aux parents et au reste de la communauté éducative, l'opposant au régime de Yaoundé adresse ses encouragements. Tout en reconnaissant leur contribution dans l'éveil de la connaissance, leur formation aux savoirs-faire, à la citoyenneté, la fraternité et la conscience patriotique. En plus de ces reconnaissances et souhaits, le leader politique se penche sur des sujets préoccupants, en particulier l'enlèvement d'enfants, et insiste sur les précautions à prendre pour mettre les enfants à l'abri. Face au phénomène, la prudence et la vigilance sont les clés que l'auteur du message recommande d'utiliser. « Parents, accompagnons et protégeons davantage nos enfants », interpelle l'enseignante des universités, non sans oublier les enseignants à qui il demande d'avoir « une conscience aiguë » et de briller par « l'exemplarité » dans l'exercice de leur métier. items.body: © CRTV Ce 07 septembre est jour de rentrée scolaire pour les élèves de la maternelle, du primaire et du secondaire. L'année scolaire débute avec des objectifs et des défis. C'est un nouveau départ pour la communauté éducative. Après trois mois de vacances, les campus scolaires reprennent vie. Les élèves de la maternelle, du primaire et du secondaire, principaux occupants de ces espaces de dispensation et d'acquisition des connaissances sont de retour. Ils sont environ neuf millions de d'enfants et d'adolescents qui sont attendus cette année dans les écoles, les lycées et collèges, dont environ 6 557 400 élèves dans l’éducation de base. Dès ce lundi, les programmes prévoient le début des cours par les la détermination du niveau des élèves et l'administration des correctifs pour ceux qui présentent des lacunes. Au niveau de l'éducation de base, le ministre Laurent Serges Etoundi Ngoa insiste sur l'atteinte des objectifs au premier rang desquels savoir lire, savoir écrire, savoir faire des calculs. Pour ce dernier élément, le membre du gouvernement entend faire former des enfants pour être aptes à effectuer des calculs sans recourir à la machine. Aux enseignements secondaires, l'intelligence artificielle ainsi que le numérique en général constituent des axes d'engagements pour cette nouvelle année. Au moment où les cours reprennent, les questions de sécurité se posent encore dans les régions du Nord-Ouest, du Sud-Ouest où du fait de la crise, les séparatistes imposent les villes mortes chaque lundi. Ainsi que dans la région de l'Extrême-Nord où des éléments de Boko Haram attaquent encore et enlèvent des personnes. Aussi, des inondations, la présence du choléra dans certaines parties du Septentrion, de même que l'insécurité dans les grandes villes sont autant de défis qui s'imposent cette année. Mais, malgré ces défis, les enseignants et responsables d'établissements sont appelés à respecter le calendrier de l'année scolaire fixé par le gouvernement. Cet article Cameroun : les élèves reprennent le chemin de l’école est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Amnesty International To Tinubu Govt: 37 Kaduna Worshippers Abducted During Easter Service Still In Captivity After Five Months
items.summary: Amnesty International To Tinubu Govt: 37 Kaduna Worshippers Abducted During Easter Service Still In Captivity After Five Months Amnesty International said the incident was one of several attacks demonstrating what it described as the “utter failure of Nigerian authorities to protect the people.”
items.body:
Amnesty International said the incident was one of several attacks demonstrating what it described as the “utter failure of Nigerian authorities to protect the people.”

Amnesty International has raised the alarm over the continued captivity of 37 worshippers abducted during raids on churches in Southern Kaduna, accusing the Nigerian government of failing to adequately protect citizens from recurring attacks, abductions and killings.

This comes despite assurances by President Bola Tinubu's administration that it is doing everything possible to protect citizens and secure the release of abductees.

The rights organisation on Monday, said the victims were abducted during Easter Sunday worship on April 5, 2026, in Ariko community, Kachia Local Government Area of Kaduna State, and have remained in captivity for five months.

Amnesty International said the incident was one of several attacks demonstrating what it described as the “utter failure of Nigerian authorities to protect the people.”

It said the prolonged captivity of the worshippers had been compounded by worsening conditions, with three of the 11 people abducted from Awon community reportedly dying in captivity within the week.

According to the organisation, a woman identified as Joy Samuel died on August 28 after giving birth in what it described as a deplorable condition. The baby she delivered also died.

It added that Mr. Yusuf Bawa, 34, and his five-year-old son also died in captivity as a result of severe illness and hunger.

“Three of the 11 people abducted from Awon community have died in captivity this week. A woman Joy Samuel died on 28 August, after giving birth in a deplorable condition. The baby she delivered also died. Mr. Yusuf Bawa 34, and his 5-year-old son have also died as a result of severe illness and hunger,” Amnesty International said.

The organisation said the deaths and illnesses suffered by the abducted persons reflected the harsh conditions and abuses they were allegedly being subjected to while in captivity.

“Deaths and severe illness these people are facing in captivity show the atrocities they are being subjected to,” it said.

Amnesty International further alleged that the victims were being subjected to repeated threats, starvation, sexual violence, beatings and other forms of degrading treatment.

“While in captivity, the abducted persons are always repeatedly threatened to be killed, starved, women and girls raped, beaten and dehumanized in so many ways,” the organisation said.

The rights group also expressed concern over the wider security situation in Southern Kaduna, saying recurring attacks, abductions for ransom and killings had continued to disrupt the lives of residents.

It said the insecurity had created a climate of fear that was affecting farming, education and other aspects of social life in communities across the region.

“Recurring attacks, abductions for ransom, and killings are continuing to make life a hell in many parts of southern Kaduna. A climate of fear is affecting agricultural activities, education and other aspects of social lives of the people,” Amnesty International said.

The organisation said the continued captivity of the worshippers underscored the need for the Nigerian government to intensify efforts to protect civilians and secure the release of people held by armed groups.

Amnesty International called on the government to fulfil its national and international human rights obligations by taking urgent steps to secure the safe release of the abducted worshippers.

“The Nigerian government must deliver on its national and international human rights obligations by immediately redoubling efforts to ensure the safe release and return of not only the 37 worshippers abducted in Kachia LGA, but also all people held captive by gunmen across Nigeria,” it said.

The organisation's concerns come as communities in Southern Kaduna continue to face security challenges, with attacks and abductions threatening livelihoods and access to education while leaving families of victims in prolonged uncertainty over the fate of their loved ones.

SaharaReporters reported in April that the Ariko community was plunged into mourning on Easter Sunday when suspected terrorists launched coordinated attacks on two churches, First ECWA Church and St. Augustine Catholic Church, killing at least seven worshippers and abducting several others.

Confirming the attack, the Councillor representing Awon Ward, Mark Bawa, said heavily armed assailants had stormed the area during early morning services.

items.title: Review: Historian Traces Boko Haram Back to Northern Nigeria’s Islamic History
items.summary: In a new book, academic historian Prof. Moses Ebe Ochonu argues that Boko Haram didn't invent its ideology from scratch but instead borrowed Dan Fodio’s 19th-century legacy to legitimise a different war with foreign inspiration. The post Review: Historian Traces Boko Haram Back to Northern Nigeria’s Islamic History appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Boko Haram has been explained in over a dozen different ways in the past 17 years since it turned violent. Several factors – such as poverty, political exclusion, corruption, climate change, state violence, foreign jihadist influence, and failed governance – have been blamed. Each of these explanations gets at something real, but none of them quite answers why the movement took root in northeastern Nigeria specifically, how it justified its violence in Islamic terms, or why some audiences bought the message while most rejected it. In his recently released book, “ Boko Haram: The Past of the Present Upheaval ”, Moses Ebe Ochonu , a Nigerian professor of African History, looks into the issue long before Boko Haram waged its first attack. Instead of treating the insurgency as a modern phenomenon, Prof. Moses traces it through nearly two centuries of arguments over Islamic authority, reform, and political legitimacy in northern Nigeria. The cover page of Prof. Moses Ochonu’s book, “Boko Haram: The Past of the Present Upheaval”. In his words, “Boko Haram did not emerge in a historical vacuum. For this reason, the complex religious, political, and socioeconomic processes that birthed the movement should be examined within the long trajectory of Islamic reform and counterreform in Northern Nigeria.” (pp. 5–6) His recent work is among the more historically grounded studies of the insurgency. In putting together the book, he used Arabic texts, colonial archives, jihadist propaganda, and decades of Sokoto Caliphate scholarship to argue that Boko Haram sits inside a much longer line of reformist movements that have fought over what Islamic governance should look like in Northern Nigeria. The book does not claim a straight intellectual line runs from the 19th Sokoto jihad to Boko Haram. What it tries to show is how the militants kept invoking Usman dan Fodio’s memory to bolster their own claim to religious legitimacy. The real contribution of the book lies in showing that the fight over Boko Haram was never just a fight over territory or doctrine, but a fight over history’s legacy — a struggle to claim that what the Sokoto jihad left behind is what Boko Haram is trying to restore. History as a weapon Prof. Moses’ argument rests on the premise that Dan Fodio occupies an important position in the region’s religious imagination, with almost every sect seeking to associate itself with him. Dan Fodio not only founded the Sokoto Caliphate; his descendants include the current Sultan of Sokoto, and his writings still carry weight in Islamic scholarship across West Africa. The book shows how both the founder of Boko Haram , Mohammed Yusuf, and its most violent leader, Abubakar Shekau , leaned on Dan Fodio’s name in their sermons and propaganda, framing colonialism and the modern Nigerian state as a break from an earlier Islamic order founded by Dan Fodio and which their movement claimed to be restoring. Their attempt to tie Boko Haram to the Sokoto jihad was deliberately designed to give them a way to fit a new insurgency into a story northern Nigerians already knew. A screenshot from one video in which Mohammed Yusuf was delivering a sermon and clips of other Boko Haram-related incidents. To expose that, the book quotes Mohammed Yusuf in one of his speeches, claiming that during Dan Fodio’s time “it was the Shari’a that was the practice in this country. Dan Fodio and other Islamic scholars carried out the jihad and ensured that Qur’anic law was implemented. Allah did not interfere with this situation until when our Muslim leaders accepted… the Europeans’ secular constitution.” (p. 3) However, Mohammed’s argument relies on a selective and fundamentally dishonest reading of history. Prof. Moses exposes the Boko Haram leader’s historical reference as a performance rather than a genuine doctrinal inheritance. Furthermore, the book distinguishes historical continuity from theological continuity because they are not the same thing. A clear line is shown between political symbolism and doctrinal influence. Boko Haram claimed Dan Fodio’s legacy, but it grew out of a different intellectual world, with roots in 20th-century Salafi reformism , global jihadist literature, and arguments that did not yet exist in Dan Fodio’s time. Theologically, Dan Fodio worked within the Sufi spiritualism – a tradition within Islam that emphasises inner devotion and spiritual purification, Ash’ari theology – a Sunni sect that uses rationalism alongside scriptures, and Maliki jurisprudence – one of the four Sunni schools of Islamic law – dominated West African Islam during his life. Boko Haram, by constrast, belongs to the Salafi-jihadi current – an extremist ideology that combines Salafi interpretation of Islam with an emphasis of Jihad as a primary purpose of the religion, which draws on ideas from well beyond northern Nigeria and is ideologically at odds with much of what Dan Fodio stood for. Prof. Moses doesn’t reduce the movement to foreign influence, though. His argument is that Boko Haram picked and chose while combining global jihadist ideas with regional symbols that would resonate locally. That keeps the book from falling into either trap of treating Boko Haram as either purely homegrown or purely imported. “The claim here is not that there is a direct instructional value in this preexisting jihad template for Boko Haram; rather, the point is to highlight the fact that Boko Haram… see[s] [itself] as continuing in the Dan Fodio jihad tradition… This history and tradition of reform, dissidence, and jihad have collectively become an all-purpose alibi to draw on.” (p. 23) From reform to radicalisation The book covers how Islamic reform movements changed in postcolonial northern Nigeria, tracing how a reformist current hardened into one that insurgents could later claim as their own. The author devotes considerable attention to the intellectual and spiritual founder of Jama’atu Izalatil Bidi’a Wa Iqamatus Sunnah (Izala), Sheikh Mahmud Gumi, and to the reformist currents that pushed back against established Sufi institutions in the latter half of the 20th century. Gumi’s movement reshaped religious debate across northern Nigeria and introduced new forms of scriptural literalism that influenced later generations. “Gumi was instrumental to the long process of Islamic dissidence that transformed the Northern Nigerian Muslim landscape from a predominantly Sufi one to one that came to be suffused in anti-Sufi [ideas].” (pp. 95-96) Even so, one notices that the author is careful not to draw a straight line from reform to violence. Reformist Salafism did not cause extremism, but he argues it changed the religious landscape enough that more radical figures later found room to claim authority within it. He notes that many scholars associated with reformist Salafism rejected armed rebellion outright, yet the intellectual climate they helped create still left an opening that more militant voices eventually filled. “The theological creeds of the Salafi clerics and the religious activists who embraced political Islam did not emerge from a historical void… While the analysis of this historical tapestry is not intended to be read as a linear progression, I argue that the ideational transformations resulting from successive reformist projects made the Boko Haram moment, if not Boko Haram itself, possible.” (p. 10) Abubakar Shekau. The book also examines how Boko Haram justified violence. Prof. Moses places the insurgency’s arguments inside long-running debates over governance, apostasy, religious reform, and what Muslim rulers owe their subjects. Readers may reject the movement’s conclusions, but the book insists its ideology can be still be understood rather than dismissed without examination. That framing, according to the author, also explains why Boko Haram kept reaching for local historical references even while aligning itself with global Salafi-jihadist networks. Groups tied to al-Qaeda or the Islamic State bring transnational frameworks with them, but they still need local stories to establish credibility in the places where they actually operate. In northern Nigeria, the memory of the Sokoto Caliphate became that story for Boko Haram. On ISWAP The closing chapters briefly turn to the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP). Prof. Moses draws a line between ISWAP and Jama’atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda’awati Wal-Jihad (JAS) —Boko Haram’s formal name. Rather than leaning mainly on indiscriminate violence, ISWAP has put more effort into building administrative structures, collecting taxes, and cultivating ties with the civilians under its influence. “The former [ISWAP] predicated its decision to split from the latter [Shekau’s JAS] on Shekau’s flagrant flouting of jihad rules, which it interpreted as a debasement of the jihad ideal. The distinction between the tactics of Boko Haram’s two factions is significant and has become the major touchstone of the ongoing scorched-earth clashes betwe

items.title: UN envoy presses Sudan leader on truce and prisoner exchange
items.summary: The UN special envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, has urged de-escalation of hostilities, and the... The post UN envoy presses Sudan leader on truce and prisoner exchange appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: The UN special envoy for Sudan, Pekka Haavisto, has urged de-escalation of hostilities, and the protection of civilians in talks with Sudan’s army chief and Sovereignty Council chair, Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan, while raising the prospect of exchanging prisoners and civilian detainees. Haavisto held a series of meetings in Khartoum on Sunday with Burhan, who heads the Sovereign Council and the army, Prime Minister Kamil Idris, Finance Minister and Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) leader Jibril Ibrahim, focusing on developments in the country, reducing tensions, ongoing consultations on dialogue, and ways to end the war and achieve peace in Sudan. In a statement after meeting El Burhan, Haavisto says dialogue is the path to sustainable peace and a comprehensive ceasefire. He says he is ready to cooperate and engage closely with all Sudanese parties and stakeholders, and to work with partners in the Quintet to advance the political process, ensuring that it is inclusive, integrated, and responsive to the aspirations of the Sudanese people. Haavisto says he conveyed important messages to El Burhan concerning de-escalation and the protection of civilians. “I look forward to continuing our meetings towards an exchange of prisoners and civilian detainees, in close cooperation with the International Committee of the Red Cross,” he says. Kamil Idris during his meeting with Pekka Haavisto in Khartoum on Sunday, September 6, 2026 (Soverignty Council Media) Sovereignty first Prime Minister Kamil Idris told the UN envoy that Sudan’s leadership will not compromise on national sovereignty or sovereign decision-making, stressing the country’s complete rejection of all forms of foreign intervention. Jibril Ibrahim told the envoy that the Sudanese Armed Forces are the national institution constitutionally responsible for protecting the country and defending its sovereignty and territorial integrity. JEM rejects wider arms embargo Ibrahim says the Justice and Equality Movement (JEM) rejects proposals to expand the arms embargo currently imposed on Darfur to cover the whole of Sudan. Such a measure, he says, would conflict with national sovereignty and restrict the armed forces’ ability to carry out their constitutional duty of protecting the country. He calls on the United Nations to welcome and support the Sudanese dialogue initiative, and to work with Sudanese parties to develop it into an inclusive, Sudanese-owned political process capable of ending the war and laying the foundations for lasting peace and a stable state. Dr. Jibril Ibrahim, head of the Justice and Equality Movement and Minister of Finance, during his meeting with UN envoy Pekka Haavisto on Sunday, September 6, 2026 (Photo: Supplied) Note: This report has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. items.title: Libya arrests five people in connection with drone strikes on refinery
items.summary: Authorities in western Libya have arrested five people including foreigners who were involved in a recent string of drone attacks on a major energy complex, the Tripoli-based government said on Sunday.
items.body:
Authorities in western Libya have arrested five people in connection with a recent string of drone attacks on a major energy facility.

The government said the arrests exposed a “vast plot” and described the attacks as part of a coordinated campaign.

Authorities said the group were part of a "sabotage cell" who also planned to attack a power station south of Tripoli, as well as other vital facilities.

They said foreigners are among the suspects but didn’t give further details.

In August, a large petrol reservoir in Zawiya caught fire during a drone attack on a major oil facility near Tripoli, Libya's state-owned oil company NOC said.

The reservoir is part of the second-largest oil refinery in Libya, with a refining capacity of 120,000 barrels per day. Other drone attacks followed at the Zawiya complex, which is located some 45 kilometres west of Tripoli.

On Thursday, another attack on fuel tanks outside of Tripoli was thwarted, the NOC said.

Libya has the largest oil reserves in Africa. But the country has been beset by violence and instability since the overthrow of Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.

Two governments are currently vying for power: the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, and a rival in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

items.title: Opinion| South Sudan cannot be governed through fear, division, and perpetual transition
items.summary: South Sudan has now spent far too many years trapped in a cycle of political The post Opinion| South Sudan cannot be governed through fear, division, and perpetual transition appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: South Sudan has now spent far too many years trapped in a cycle of political crisis, insecurity, poverty, corruption allegations, and unfinished peace agreements. For more than a decade, the people of South Sudan have been promised peace, democracy, development, and accountable government, yet ordinary citizens continue to bear the consequences of political failure. Salva Kiir and those who continue to defend his government must answer a simple question: after all these years, where is the political, economic, and social transformation that South Sudanese were promised? Even in Warrap, Salva Kiir’s traditional political stronghold, public frustration cannot simply be dismissed. No community should be expected to support a government forever merely because its leader comes from that community. Loyalty based on ethnicity or regional identity cannot replace good governance, security, development, accountability, and respect for human dignity. The same principle applies everywhere in South Sudan. The people of Equatoria, Upper Nile, Bahr el Ghazal, and every other part of the country are citizens of one republic known as South Sudan. They are not political territories belonging to individual leaders or political parties. The 2026 elections must not become another political maneuver South Sudan is again approaching elections, currently scheduled for December 2026. But the central question is not simply whether elections will technically take place. The real question is whether South Sudan will create the political and security conditions necessary for credible, inclusive, peaceful and genuinely competitive elections . Even the United Nations has warned that the political environment remains fragile and that important conditions for credible elections have yet to be secured. UN officials have specifically raised concerns about the absence of key opposition actors from important political processes, the lack of consensus, stalled implementation of the peace agreement, and the shrinking political space. An election without political freedom is not democracy. An election in which opposition leaders cannot freely organize, travel, campaign, and communicate with citizens is not a genuine democratic contest. An election conducted while political opponents are detained or excluded from meaningful participation cannot easily command public confidence. An election conducted without sufficient security, institutional independence, and political consensus risks becoming another source of conflict rather than a peaceful mechanism for transferring political power. The lesson of 2013 and 2016 must not be forgotten. South Sudanese people remember what happened after the political crisis within the SPLM in 2013 and the return to fighting in 2016. The 2016 violence was not an abstract political disagreement. It produced deaths, displacement, destruction, forced disappearance, and immense human suffering. The Revitalized Peace Agreement of 2018 was supposed to prevent South Sudan from returning to that cycle. Yet the implementation of the agreement remains incomplete. UNMISS reports that the transitional period has been extended repeatedly and that the implementation of the peace agreement remains unfinished. That is why South Sudan cannot afford another political confrontation disguised as an electoral process. The country needs political competition—not political elimination. It needs debate—not intimidation. It needs an independent judiciary—not a judiciary perceived as serving political interests. It needs professional security institutions—not security forces used as instruments of political competition. It needs elections in which every legitimate political actor can compete according to the law. Dr. Riek Machar’s political rights cannot simply be wished away Whether someone supports Dr. Riek Machar or opposes him is a political choice. But whether he and other South Sudanese citizens are entitled to political rights is a matter of law. The detention and subsequent trial of Dr. Machar have already become a major concern in the peace process. UNMISS called for restraint and respect for the Revitalized Peace Agreement following his detention in March 2025. More recent UN reporting has continued to identify his detention and trial as major factors contributing to the political crisis. No political leader should be forced to surrender his political rights simply because his participation may be inconvenient to those currently exercising power. If Dr. Riek Machar has committed a criminal offense, the answer must be lawful, independent, and fair judicial proceedings , not political conditions requiring him to abandon political life. If he has not committed such an offense, then continued political detention cannot be justified merely because his political participation is considered a threat. The same standard must apply to every South Sudanese politician—whether they belong to the SPLM, SPLM-IO, a smaller opposition party, civil society, or any other political movement. What international law says The political rights of South Sudanese citizens are not gifts from Salva Kiir, Dr. Riek Machar, the SPLM, SPLM-IO, or any political organization. International human rights law protects them. Article 21 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides that everyone has the right to participate in the government of his or her country, directly or through freely chosen representatives, and that the will of the people shall be expressed through periodic and genuine elections based on universal and equal suffrage. Article 19 of the UDHR protects freedom of opinion and expression, while Article 20 protects peaceful assembly and association. The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) similarly protects political participation, peaceful assembly, and freedom of association. The UN Human Rights Committee has emphasized that political participation and peaceful assembly are closely connected. Most importantly for South Sudan as an African state, Article 13 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights provides: “Every citizen shall have the right to participate freely in the government of his country, either directly or through freely chosen representatives…” The African Charter also protects freedom of expression under Article 9, freedom of association under Article 10, and peaceful assembly under Article 11. The African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance further emphasizes regular, transparent, free and fair elections, political pluralism, participation of citizens, transparency, accountability, respect for human rights, and the role of opposition political parties. These principles matter because democracy is not simply about putting a ballot box somewhere and telling citizens to vote. Democracy requires a political environment in which citizens are genuinely free to choose. South Sudan does not belong to one man or one tribe South Sudan belongs to its people. It does not belong to Kiir. It does not belong to Machar. It does not belong to SPLM. It does not belong to SPLM-IO. It does not belong to the Jieng Council of Elders. It does not belong to any tribe, military faction, political party, or political family. It belongs to the South Sudanese people. Therefore, nobody should fear a genuinely competitive election. If a political leader believes that the people support him, the most legitimate way to demonstrate that support is through a free, fair, transparent, and credible election . The people—not the army, not political appointments, not detention, not ethnic mobilization, and not government propaganda—should decide who governs South Sudan. The people deserve more than 21 years of political survival South Sudanese citizens deserve functioning hospitals, schools, roads, clean water, electricity, employment, security, justice and a government capable of paying its workers. They deserve a state in which public resources are used for public purposes. They deserve institutions that work. They deserve an independent judiciary. They deserve security forces that protect citizens rather than frighten them. They deserve political leaders who can be challenged without turning political disagreement into ethnic conflict. And, above all, they deserve the opportunity to choose their leaders peacefully. Egypt has demonstrated how quickly a state can transform parts of its infrastructure and build major national projects when political will and resources are mobilized. South Sudan, despite enormous oil wealth and international assistance, continues to struggle with basic services and infrastructure. The question therefore remains: How much longer can our people be asked to wait? NO MORE POLITICAL EXCLUSION Dr. Riek Machar’s political future should not be determined by President Kiir, the security apparatus, political elders, or any other individual or group. It should be determined under South Sudan’s constitutional and legal frame

items.title: Displaced people living under dire conditions in Sudan’s Blue Nile State
items.summary: The humanitarian situation has worsened for dozens of families displaced from the town of Qaysan The post Displaced people living under dire conditions in Sudan’s Blue Nile State appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: The humanitarian situation has worsened for dozens of families displaced from the town of Qaysan in Blue Nile State in Sudan. They fled fighting and are now living under trees in the Khor al-Qana area, east of Wad al-Mahi locality. According to local estimates, approximately 150 families are living under trees in Khor al-Qana, in extremely difficult conditions, lacking shelter, food, and necessities. Several displaced people told Radio Tamazuj that their humanitarian situation is rapidly deteriorating due to the lack of necessities. They appealed to humanitarian agencies and organizations to intervene urgently and provide food and shelter. One displaced person pointed out that their suffering is exacerbated by the lack of shelter, and urgently requested blankets and tarpaulins to protect themselves and their children from the harsh weather. Displaced person Farouk Adam said that displaced families have not received any aid or assistance so far, calling for the urgent provision of relief supplies and necessities. For her part, displaced person Hafsa Ismail said the humanitarian situation is “extremely dire,” noting that they fled the fighting and left everything behind, only to find themselves now without food or shelter. The conditions of the displaced in Khor al-Qana reflect the growing humanitarian needs of civilians fleeing the fighting in the Blue Nile region, as the exodus continues in search of safer areas. The post Displaced people living under dire conditions in Sudan’s Blue Nile State appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .

items.title: Sudan: UN envoy urges progress toward inclusive political process
items.summary: U.N. envoy to Sudan Pekka Haavisto on Sunday called for progress toward an “inclusive and The post Sudan: UN envoy urges progress toward inclusive political process appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: U.N. envoy to Sudan Pekka Haavisto on Sunday called for progress toward an “inclusive and strategic” political process to help end the country’s war. Haavisto made the remarks during talks in Khartoum with army chief and Sovereign Council Chairman Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, according to a statement issued by the council. The two discussed the security and political situation in Sudan, efforts to strengthen stability and prospects for a comprehensive peace, the statement said. “I conveyed important messages related to de-escalation and the protection of civilians,” Haavisto was quoted as saying. He also voiced hope that continued talks could lead to the exchange of prisoners and civilian detainees held by the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). “Dialogue is the path to sustainable peace,” Haavisto said, adding that the United Nations would work with Sudanese stakeholders and partners in the five-member mechanism to advance a political process reflecting the aspirations of the Sudanese people. The mechanism comprises the United Nations, African Union, European Union, Arab League and Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD). Haavisto arrived in Sudan on Friday for talks with the parties involved in the conflict on efforts to de-escalate fighting and protect civilians. On Aug. 30, Sudan’s Dialogue Preparatory Committee launched an independent initiative aimed at facilitating consultations and helping lay the groundwork for ending the war and building broader national consensus. Sudan has been at war since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the army and the RSF. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to U.N. and international estimates. items.title: Op-Ed: Peace in Sudan requires an expanded weapons embargo
items.summary: Sudan has been descending into hell for years. The United Nations Security Council now has The post Op-Ed: Peace in Sudan requires an expanded weapons embargo appeared first on Radio Tamazuj .
items.body: Sudan has been descending into hell for years. The United Nations Security Council now has a chance to do right by the people of Sudan and remember what it was created to do: stop wars, keep the peace, and protect lives. But it can do those things only if its members are willing to step up. Sudan is experiencing the world’s worst humanitarian crisis. More than 33 million people are in need of basic assistance. An estimated 19.5 million people, disproportionately women and children, face acute hunger. Almost 9 million people have now been driven from their homes, another 4.5 million have fled the country, and at least 150,000 are dead. Yet somehow, this historic catastrophe has generated little more than horrified whispers from the West’s most vaunted institutions. The Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its allied militias have committed genocide, murdering men and boys on an ethnic basis and raping women and girls. The U.N. estimates that more than 12 million Sudanese women and girls—roughly half the country’s female population—are at risk of sexual violence. The Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have committed atrocities, too. More than 130 humanitarian workers have been killed since the war began. Both sides loot and block food, aid, and other supplies. They also brandish access to lifesaving aid as a tool of suppression, with the lives of local recipients hanging in the balance. And now, with the advent of drone warfare, both sides are finding it easier and cheaper to inflict more lethal damage. Last year, at least 2,670 people, a number that includes combatants and civilians, were killed in drone attacks. That represents a 600 percent increase in drone-related deaths over a single year. In just the first five months of this year, drones killed more than 1,000 people, making up roughly 80 percent of civilian deaths during that period. Markets, hospitals, schools, and aid routes have become fair game for thugs with remote controls. The barrier to entry for mass violence in Sudan has never been lower, yet the U.N. is policing the conflict with an arms embargo written more than two decades ago. Security Council Resolution 1591, which imposed an arms embargo on Darfur in 2005, is older than Apple’s iPhone—let alone the drones hovering above Sudan today. The international community’s approach to Sudan has simply not kept up with the times. First, there’s the battlefield. The war has spread into the Kordofan region and Blue Nile state. The Security Council’s embargo stops at Darfur, several hundred miles away from the new arenas of conflict. Then there’s the international meddling, which has undoubtedly prolonged the fighting and heightened the heavy toll on civilians. More than a dozen countries with diverse motives are providing some form of military support to the warring parties. Mercenaries have been recruited from as far away as Colombia. Foreign networks of all stripes supply drones, weapons, parts, money, and their own renditions of expertise. Munitions do not become duds and drones do not fall out of the sky if they cross imaginary embargo lines on maps, for example, where Kordofan begins and Darfur ends. Neither do smugglers sit on their hands when they can move weapons from other parts of Sudan. They adapt—just as the RSF and SAF have. But the U.N. has failed to adapt. For more than 20 years, the Security Council has kept the same geographic embargo in place while the battlefield, the weapons, and the players supplying them have shifted unrecognizably. That’s why the G-7—including the United States—has called on the Security Council to expand the embargo across all of Sudan. So let’s do it. The United States has presented a resolution to the Security Council that would expand the arms embargo nationwide, making clear that sanctions and member state implementation of those rules apply to all the networks keeping this war alive—on both sides, with no carve-outs. Yes, it will even apply to the arms traffickers, procurement agents, mercenary recruiters, state-backed patrons, established financiers, drone suppliers, and genocidal commanders who have for so long evaded justice. Already, some on the Security Council are posturing to oppose or abstain from this resolution. They may try to portray this embargo as taking sides in Sudan’s civil war. Others may try to deny their own direct involvement in Sudan, suggesting instead that private traders and intermediaries are responsible for the flow of weapons into the country. There is irony in both arguments. For one, the new blanket embargo would apply to the RSF, the SAF, and any actors that feed either side munitions. If anything, evangelizing the current embargo, evidently porous and incomplete as it is, betrays that those warning against “taking sides” already have. Then there’s the cognitive dissonance in blaming rogue traders and freelance brokers as the real culprits while opposing a resolution designed to reach precisely those actors. If private financiers, smugglers, and unofficial procurement networks are really to blame, then help us identify them, sanction them, block their arms trafficking, and shut them down. A government that truly has nothing to hide should have no objection helping the U.N. monitor and close arms channels it claims are operating beyond its control. Under President Donald Trump, the United States has already gone to work. We have sanctioned individuals and entities facilitating mercenary recruitment, foreign fighters, procurement, and other support to this war. Other countries should do the same at and beyond the U.N. Think of this resolution as a rubric. Those tearing Sudan apart will be graded for their actions. But it will still be the member states that must enforce consequences. The U.N. will monitor violations, identify the networks moving weapons, and document who flouts the embargo. And for member states, most of which place a premium on acting pursuant to clear U.N. authority, this resolution removes any ambiguity or excuse. With the Security Council’s mandate behind them, member states can—and should—stop shipments, freeze assets, tighten export controls, and move against the networks violating the embargo. In the end, Sudan’s warring parties must still stand down. We, for our part, believe they should do so via a humanitarian truce that the United States has proposed alongside a U.N. mechanism to deliver aid and create space for a broader peace process. As long as weapons are easier to come by than food in Sudan, cooler heads have little chance to prevail. And it appears that some on the Security Council are just fine with that. Any Security Council member considering abstaining or voting no should understand what it is voting for. It will mean business as usual in Sudan—and all the wanton violence that entails. At best, vetoes and abstentions alike turn a blind eye to drones bombing hospitals and markets, aid blocked from starving families, and millions of innocents paying the price for others’ geopolitical voyeurism. At worst, those who would veto or abstain should welcome the question: Why are you aiding and abetting those on either side who are destroying Sudan, its people, and its future? Neither the RSF nor the SAF has any legitimate claim to govern Sudan when this war ends. Both have committed atrocities against the Sudanese people, and both have forfeited any suggestion that they possess political legitimacy. Sudan’s future cannot belong to whichever armed faction is left standing. It must come from a credible, independent civilian dialogue that gives the Sudanese people themselves—not the men with the most guns or the deadliest drones—a say over their future. The United States will not rubber-stamp another year of descension into hell. We and the world will note who stands with the Sudanese people and who stands against them. Michael Waltz is the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. He previously served as a U.S. representative from Florida, national security advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, and in the U.S. Army as a combat-decorated Green Beret. Massad Boulos is a senior advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump for Arab and African affairs. He advises the president on regional diplomacy and leads U.S. engagement on key political, security, and economic priorities, including efforts to end the war in Sudan. items.title: Cape Verde declares mourning for 25 crash victims as Nigeria grows numb to daily deaths
items.summary: CAPE VERDE has declared two days of national mourning after a bus crash on the island of Fogo killed at least 25 people, most of them children and teenagers. The crash occurred on Saturday evening, September 5, as the bus was returning from an excursion to Chã das Caldeiras, a settlement located within the volcanic […] The post Cape Verde declares mourning for 25 crash victims as Nigeria grows num
items.body:
CAPE VERDE has declared two days of national mourning after a bus crash on the island of Fogo killed at least 25 people, most of them children and teenagers.

The crash occurred on Saturday evening, September 5, as the bus was returning from an excursion to Chã das Caldeiras, a settlement located within the volcanic caldera of Pico do Fogo.

The vehicle was travelling along the mountainous route between Chã das Caldeiras and Campanas de Cima when it reportedly veered off the road and plunged down a steep, rocky ravine.

Local reports said the bus fell about 30 metres into the ravine, making rescue operations difficult because of the rugged and inaccessible terrain.

At least 25 people were killed in the crash, including the driver. The bus was reportedly carrying 32 people at the time of the accident.

Most of those aboard were young people, with reports identifying many of the victims as secondary school students from the communities of Curral Grande and Ponta Verde.

The bus driver was also reported to have organised the annual excursion for the children. Reports said he transported some of the pupils to school during the academic term and organised the outing privately as a gift to them.

The difficult terrain around the crash site complicated the operation, with rescuers having to work in a steep, rocky ravine that could not be easily reached by vehicles.

Seven of the victims were buried early on Sunday because of the condition of their bodies, according to local authorities and media reports.

The injured survivors were taken to the São Francisco de Assis Regional Hospital on Fogo for treatment. Reports have given different figures for the number of injured people receiving treatment, with some saying around 12 survivors were taken to hospital and others putting the number higher.

Some of the injured were reported to be in serious condition.

The scale of the tragedy prompted authorities to declare a period of mourning across the island and the country.

Prime Minister Francisco Carvalho reportedly announced two days of mourning on Sunday as the country came to terms with the deaths.

President José Maria Pereira Neves also expressed condolences to the families of the victims and described the crash as “a great catastrophe.”

Neves said the immediate priority was to support the affected families and communities, while authorities were expected to investigate the circumstances surrounding the crash.

The cause of the accident had not been officially established as of Sunday. Authorities were investigating how the bus left the road and plunged into the ravine.

The tragedy has also led to the cancellation of some religious festivities on the island as communities mourned the victims.

Funeral ceremonies began on Sunday, with 18 coffins reportedly displayed during a Mass at São Lourenço Church before burial ceremonies continued.

The accident has shocked Cape Verde, an Atlantic island nation off the coast of West Africa where large-scale road crashes are relatively uncommon.

Fogo is one of Cape Verde’s volcanic islands and is dominated by Pico do Fogo, the country’s highest peak. Chã das Caldeiras is located within the volcano’s caldera and is a popular destination for visitors and excursions.

The tragedy in Cape Verde contrasts with Nigeria’s recurring experience of mass deaths from terrorism, banditry, kidnapping and communal violence, where dozens of people are often killed in individual attacks and hundreds more lose their lives over relatively short periods.

For many Nigerians, however, the frequency of such attacks has made mass death an increasingly familiar part of daily life, as families continue to bury victims of attacks.

Unlike Cape Verde’s declaration of two days of national mourning following the deaths of 25 people in a single accident, Nigeria rarely declares national mourning over individual incidents of terrorist attacks, communal killings, or related tragedies, despite the cumulative toll of violence across the country. The government often resorts to issuing condolences and directive to security operatives.

Mustapha Usman is an investigative journalist with the International Centre for Investigative Reporting. You can easily reach him via: musman@icirnigeria.com. He tweets @UsmanMustapha_M

items.title: Somali cleric Ali Wajis endorses killing of government critics
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent pro-government religious scholar told a gathering of senior Somali officials, including the defense minister, on Sunday that people who oppose the administration of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud should be treated as terrorists and killed – a statement that has alarmed opposition figures already on edge after a drone strike wounded […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – A prominent pro-government religious scholar told a gathering of senior Somali officials, including the defense minister, on Sunday that people who oppose the administration of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud should be treated as terrorists and killed – a statement that has alarmed opposition figures already on edge after a drone strike wounded a former security chief turned government critic on Thursday. Sheikh Ali Wajis, a cleric known for his consistent public backing of the Federal Government, made the remarks at a meeting attended by government officials, including the Minister of Defense. “Anyone who fights Somalia’s current government should face the same punishment as terrorists and should be killed,” Wajis told the gathering. Neither Wajis nor the Ministry of Defense could be reached for comment. Villa Somalia had not issued a statement responding to the remarks as of publication, and no official who attended Sunday’s meeting has publicly distanced the government from them. Coming on the heels of an attack on an opposition figure Wajis’s remarks land just days after a strike on the residence of Gen. Mahad Abdirahman Aden , widely known as “Taliye Shub,” in the border town of Doolow, in the Gedo region. Gen. Mahad, Somalia’s former Custodial Corps commander, was wounded in the attack along with his wife and several others; at least one person, reported to be an Ethiopian domestic worker, was killed. He was evacuated for treatment across the border in Ethiopia. Gen. Mahad, who was removed from his post earlier this year and briefly placed under house arrest, has since emerged as a vocal critic of the Federal Government and is aligned with the political camp of former Southwest State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Laftagareen.” Authorities in Jubaland have accused Turkish military aircraft of carrying out the strike, calling it a deliberate, politically motivated attack tied to Gen. Mahad’s opposition to Mogadishu. In a statement, Jubaland said two missiles were fired, with one also striking the residence of Doolow’s district commissioner. The Federal Government has denied any involvement in an airstrike, offering a different account of what caused the damage to the house. Turkey, which has become one of Somalia’s most significant military partners, providing training, equipment and air support, has not publicly responded to the accusation. The disputed strike triggered protests in Doolow, with residents demanding an independent investigation into who was responsible and why Gen. Mahad’s residence was targeted. A cleric with a history of hardline rhetoric This is not the first time Wajis, who has served as an adviser to successive Somali administrations, has taken a hardline public stance in defense of the government. In April, as Somali National Army desertions mounted during Al-Shabab’s offensive in the Shabelle regions, Wajis publicly branded soldiers who fled their posts as apostates and called for their arrest – remarks that were echoed at the time by a senior Custodial Corps commander, who warned that deserters and their families could face arrest or execution. His latest comments arrive at a moment of unusually sharp strain between Mogadishu and Somalia’s federal member states. Jubaland, Puntland and ousted Southwest administration have all rejected constitutional amendments extending federal institutions’ mandates, and have formally suspended ties with the Federal Government, accusing it of interference in their political and security affairs. Why it matters Coming so soon after an unresolved and contested attack on a prominent opposition-aligned general, a call from a cleric closely associated with the presidency – delivered in front of the defense minister – for opponents of the government to be killed is likely to deepen fears among opposition figures and federal member states that political dissent in Somalia is being conflated with terrorism. Independent verification of the strike’s origin, and any government response to Wajis’s remarks, remained pending as of publication. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com
