items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro departed Hargeisa on Thursday for a working visit to the United States, part of an effort to present the self-declared republic as an emerging power of geoeconomic and geosecurity value to Washington and other Western capitals, with particular emphasis on the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint. Officials said […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi Irro departed Hargeisa on Thursday for a working visit to the United States, part of an effort to present the self-declared republic as an emerging power of geoeconomic and geosecurity value to Washington and other Western capitals, with particular emphasis on the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint. Officials said Irro will make a stopover in the United Arab Emirates en route to the US. The Somaliland leader is expected to pitch his territory’s importance to Washington on two fronts: its rare earth mineral deposits and its proximity to Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint, a position officials believe could support a US military footing there and help counter threats from Houthi rebels. Somalia’s federal government has moved in parallel, dispatching a delegation led by Deputy Prime Minister Salah Jama on a counter-diplomacy push aimed at undercutting Irro’s Washington trip. The rival missions have drawn attention to the family ties binding the two camps. “For those who don’t know – Jama is actually from Somaliland and Irro’s kin,” said Rashid Abdi, a Horn of Africa analyst at Sahan Research. “Fascinating diplomacy,” Abdi added. items.title: Exiled opposition politician Khalid Omar attacks campaign promoting Burhan for president
items.summary: KHARTOUM — Exiled Sudanese opposition politician Khalid Omar Youssef on Friday attacked a campaign promoting army chief Abdelfattah al-Burhan for president, saying it showed that the country’s devastating war was ultimately a struggle for power. Omar, a former cabinet affairs minister and deputy president of the Sudanese Congress Party, made the remarks after a poster […] The post Exiled oppositio
items.body:
Former Sudanese cabinet minister and exiled opposition politician Khalid Omer Yousif, speaks during an interview with Reuters in Khartoum, Sudan January 31, 2022. [Photo by REUTERS] KHARTOUM — Exiled Sudanese opposition politician Khalid Omar Youssef on Friday attacked a campaign promoting army chief Abdelfattah al-Burhan for president, saying it showed that the country’s devastating war was ultimately a struggle for power.

Omar, a former cabinet affairs minister and deputy president of the Sudanese Congress Party, made the remarks after a poster circulated on social media bearing a photograph of Burhan and the slogan, “We want Burhan as president,” describing the call as “a popular demand.”

There was no indication that Burhan himself produced, launched or endorsed the campaign.

“With the launch of a campaign to nominate Burhan for president of the republic, we have reached the final scene of the film very quickly,” Omar wrote on his social media Facebook page. “Here is a clear answer to the question: Whose war is this, and why?”

Omar accused Burhan of pursuing political power at enormous cost to Sudan and pointed to the army chief’s role in the October 2021 military takeover that ended the civilian-led transition established after the overthrow of longtime ruler Omar al-Bashir.

“The general is hastening his steps toward achieving his dream, which has cost the country and its people dearly,” Omar said.

He accused Burhan of betraying the 2019 revolution that brought millions of Sudanese onto the streets and ultimately ended Bashir’s nearly three decades in power.

Burhan led the October 2021 takeover alongside Rapid Support Forces militia commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti. The two later fell out amid disputes over the political transition and the integration of the RSF militia into the regular army, culminating in war between their forces in April 2023.

The conflict has devastated large parts of Sudan, killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions inside and outside the country.

Omar said Burhan’s years at the head of Sudan’s military-led authorities had coincided with war, economic collapse, mass displacement and threats to the country’s unity and sovereignty.

“He should ask his predecessor, Bashir: Where did this path ultimately lead him?” Omar said.

Omar has lived in exile since leaving Sudan amid the war. He is deputy president of the Sudanese Congress Party and one of the prominent civilian politicians opposed to the conflict and to continued military rule.

He and several other civilian opposition figures have faced criminal accusations from authorities aligned with the army, which have accused anti-war politicians of supporting or providing political cover for the RSF.

The politicians have denied backing the paramilitary group and say the accusations are intended to silence opponents of the war.

Burhan has also publicly attacked some of the exiled civilian politicians and said they would not be allowed to return to Sudan.

Omar served as cabinet affairs minister in the civilian-military transitional government established after Bashir’s overthrow and remained a prominent figure in the civilian political movement following the 2021 coup.

In his statement on Friday, Omar rejected the army and its supporters’ description of the conflict as a “war of dignity,” saying the appearance of a campaign promoting Burhan for president reinforced his view that the conflict was about political power.

“This is another wake-up call for everyone who naively believed that this was a war of dignity or sovereignty,” he said. “It is a disgraceful war for power.”

Omar described the conflict as a “counter-revolution against the Sudanese people’s dream of freedom, peace and justice” and called for its rejection.

Burhan has not publicly declared that he intends to run for president, and the appearance of posters promoting him does not amount to an official candidacy. Sudan has not held a presidential election since Bashir was removed from power in April 2019.

items.title: UN report says foreign suppliers boosted drone capabilities of Sudan’s belligerents
items.summary: GENEVA — Foreign suppliers have significantly expanded the drone capabilities of both the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), allowing the warring sides to conduct increasingly sophisticated operations far beyond traditional front lines, United Nations investigators said in a report released on Thursday. The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan
items.body:
Drone attack on Port Sudan targeting an oil depot on May 5, 2025. [Photo courtesy] GENEVA — Foreign suppliers have significantly expanded the drone capabilities of both the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), allowing the warring sides to conduct increasingly sophisticated operations far beyond traditional front lines, United Nations investigators said in a report released on Thursday.

The UN Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan said foreign recruitment, weapons transfers and logistical networks operating across several countries were strengthening the military capabilities of parties to the conflict, with civilians bearing much of the cost.

The investigators documented what they described as transnational networks involved in recruiting, training and deploying foreign personnel to support the RSF, as well as facilitating transfers of weapons, ammunition and military technology.

The report also found reasonable grounds to believe that the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) had used foreign-supplied drones in military operations that harmed civilians and civilian objects.

“The consequences of this external support are being felt most acutely by civilians,” Mohamad Chande Othman, chair of the Fact-Finding Mission, said.

“This external support has not brought greater protection for civilians. Instead, civilians are paying the price through attacks on homes, hospitals, schools, markets and places of refuge.”

Sudan has been engulfed in war since April 2023, when fighting erupted between the SAF, headed by army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the RSF, commanded by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, widely known as Hemedti.

The UN investigators said foreign assistance had helped expand the use of drones by both sides, increasing their ability to conduct strikes at considerable distances from the main battlefields.

The report documented the deployment of as many as 2,000 former Colombian military contractors who it said were directly involved alongside RSF units in Darfur and Kordofan, including in the operation of combat drones, artillery and other advanced weapons.

Investigators said there were reasonable grounds to believe that private entities, recruiters and logistical facilitators operating from countries including Colombia and the United Arab Emirates used transit points in Chad, southeastern Libya and the Somali city of Bosaso to move personnel, training, weapons and logistical supplies to the RSF.

Mona Rishmawi, a member of the mission, said investigators had identified “a transnational chain of networks spanning several countries” supplying the RSF with foreign personnel, training, weapons and logistical assistance.

“This support fed into RSF operations in Zamzam camp and later during the takeover of El-Fasher, where the Mission documented grave human rights and international humanitarian law violations and international crimes, including conduct displaying hallmarks of genocide,” she said.

The findings come as drones have assumed an increasingly prominent role in Sudan’s war, allowing the belligerents to attack targets well beyond areas of direct ground combat. The mission said foreign suppliers had substantially enhanced the drone capabilities of both the SAF and RSF.

Investigators said states connected to the supply chains had obligations under international law to investigate and disrupt illicit mercenary and weapons networks operating from or through their territories and to prevent transfers that could contribute to serious violations.

The mission called for enforcement of the existing UN arms embargo on Darfur and urged the UN Security Council to extend the restrictions to the whole of Sudan. It also called for investigations into individuals and entities involved in illicit support networks.

Othman said repeated international warnings over abuses in Sudan had failed to produce sufficient action.

“Protecting civilians in Sudan requires taking action not only against those waging this war, but also against the individuals, entities, and networks that enable its continuation.”

items.title: Injuries as violence erupts at South Africa anti-migrant protest
items.summary: A demonstration against undocumented migrants in South Africa descended into violence Thursday with one foreign national arrested and a community leader saying five Congolese were hurt
items.body:
A demonstration against undocumented migrants in South Africa descended into violence Thursday with one foreign national arrested and a community leader saying five Congolese were hurt.

The protest was in the port city of Durban which has been at the epicentre of weeks of action against irregular migration in which at least four foreign nationals have been killed and tens of thousands have fled the country.

Police said about 100 marchers from an anti-illegal migrant group went on what they called "a clean-up campaign" against an encampment of several hundred foreign nationals outside a government office.

Foreigners, many of them from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), moved to the site 13 weeks ago to seek protection against mobs of South Africans campaigning against undocumented migrants.

"During the commotion, stones were thrown around, and one which was thrown by a foreign national landed on a police officer," police said.

The person was arrested, a statement said, without giving details.

A leader of the group of foreigners told AFP that five Congolese nationals including two children were hurt in the clash.

"The march today was very violent," said Bishop Raphael, who is from the DRC.

"They found us here and immediately attacked our people. We are not committing any crime by being here. This is uncalled for," he said.

Many of the people in the group claim to be refugees from the DRC.

Raphael said the protesters were armed with sticks and attempted to attack the encampment while police tried to separate them.

Police used stun grenades to disperse the crowds, resulting in the injuries, he said.

Tensions soared across South Africa after fringe groups campaigning against undocumented migrants set a June 30 deadline for them to leave.

More than 200,000 people fled, according to an AFP tally based on figures released by African governments that have repatriated their nationals.

At least four migrants were killed in that violence, according to the South African police, though some foreign governments say the toll is higher.

items.body: Taemo Hadish is a farmer in Haweleti, in Raya Zebo, Tigray region. She says her cattle have become too weak to move because of a lack of fodder, while the farmland she relies on to feed her family have failed to grow. “We have not seen rain for the whole year,” she says. “Our animals are dying because there is nothing for them to eat.” The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) has warned that parts of Ethiopia could experience below-average rainfall during the June–September rainy season as El Niño conditions develop. In northern Ethiopia, particularly Tigray, conflict-related disruptions to farming seasons have left 21 woredas at high risk of severe food insecurity, with 2.45 million people in need of emergency food assistance. Similar conditions are being reported in neighbouring Afar, where livestock are also dying as the drought worsens. According to a July FAO report, more than 18,000 livestock have died in Yaqer locality, Afar region, due to shortages of water and fodder. Farmers and woreda officials interviewed by the BBC say farmers in three woredas in Tigray region are struggling because of delayed rains linked to El Niño. The weather patterns have caused drought in the southern, south-eastern and central zones, while some woredas that received rainfall have experienced heavy hailstorms and flooding. In its May seasonal forecast, the Ethiopian Meteorology Institute warned that parts of southern and eastern Tigray, North and South Wollo, Afar and eastern Ethiopia were likely to receive below-average rainfall. It also forecast dry conditions in northern and eastern parts of the country in August. “We have never experienced a drought like this. There has not been enough rain, and we are going through a very difficult year,” says Alem Misgana, who lives in Alitena, in the Eastern Zone. Article in Amharic. items.title: Sudanese anti-war forces reject AU backing for El Burhan dialogue
items.summary: Sudanese anti-war political and civil forces have rejected the African Union’s endorsement of a “Sudanese-Sudanese... The post Sudanese anti-war forces reject AU backing for El Burhan dialogue appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: Sudanese anti-war political and civil forces have rejected the African Union’s endorsement of a “Sudanese-Sudanese Dialogue Initiative” proposed by Sovereignty Council President and Commander-in-Chief of the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) Lt Gen Abdelfattah El Burhan, warning that the process could legitimise military rule and deepen Sudan’s division. In a memorandum submitted on September 2 to the African Peace and Security Council and the AU Political Affairs, Peace and Security Commission, the groups rejected the AU Commission’s August 31 statement welcoming the initiative . They said the endorsement contradicted the Peace and Security Council’s position that a humanitarian truce should lead to an immediate and comprehensive ceasefire before any political process. They also criticised the AU for backing an initiative proposed by El Burhan, whose October 2021 military coup resulted in Sudan’s suspension from AU activities. The groups stressed that dialogue itself was not the problem but argued that any credible political process must be genuinely Sudanese-owned, with participants, agenda and timing agreed by Sudanese stakeholders. They called for the humanitarian crisis and cessation of hostilities to remain at the centre of the process. A group photo of members of the Sudanese-Sudanese Dialogue Committee after the committee’s press conference in Khartoum on Sunday, August 30, 2026 (Photo: Social media) They also demanded the exclusion of the National Congress Party, the Islamic Movement and affiliated forces, which they accused of playing a documented role in starting and prolonging the war. The memorandum warned that holding dialogue in territory controlled by one side of the conflict, without a prior ceasefire or broad participation, could entrench the political and territorial fragmentation created by the war. The groups called on the AU to explain its endorsement, reaffirm its ceasefire-first position, maintain neutrality and coordinate international mediation efforts, including the Quartet and Quintet mechanism. The AU Commission said its support was based on the need for an inclusive process involving Sudanese civil, political and societal actors. It said the dialogue should ultimately lead to a united, sovereign Sudan governed by legitimate civilian institutions, with a single national security structure and peaceful mechanisms for resolving political differences. Othman Mirghani, spokesman for the Sudanese-Sudanese Dialogue Committee, welcomed the AU statement, saying it came at a crucial stage as the committee began its work. Speaking to Radio Dabanga, Mirghani said regional backing could help secure wider international support while preserving the committee’s independence. He said the initiative sought direct dialogue among Sudanese inside the country and that the AU could help facilitate contacts with the UN, United States, UK and European Union. The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces aligned-government, Sudan Founding Alliance (Tasees) , also rejected the AU endorsement, describing it as support for the army’s position and bias towards one side of the conflict. Tasees spokesperson Ahmed Tagad Lisan said El Burhan had called for the dialogue, formed its preparatory committee and determined its agenda and venue, giving the SAF’s leadership undue influence over the process. The anti-war forces reiterated that they remain open to dialogue but insisted that a credible process must first stop the fighting, protect civilians and prevent the war from being used to legitimise competing centres of power. items.title: Laftagaren forces attack Somali army positions in Baidoa again
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted in Baidoa on Thursday after forces loyal to ousted Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked the city from multiple directions, seizing two federal army bases on its outskirts before entering the town and engaging government troops in fierce gun battles that lasted for hours. Laftagaren’s Darwish forces entered Baidoa […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Heavy fighting erupted in Baidoa on Thursday after forces loyal to ousted Southwest State President Abdiasis Laftagaren attacked the city from multiple directions, seizing two federal army bases on its outskirts before entering the town and engaging government troops in fierce gun battles that lasted for hours. Laftagaren’s Darwish forces entered Baidoa early in the morning, according to a spokesman for the forces, who said they would continue fighting until the last federal soldier leaves the region and control of the region is fully restored to its people. The forces later withdrew from the city, bringing the fighting to an end. Southwest State Information Minister Nur Sidow told reporters in Baidoa after the fighting that those who had attacked the city were Al-Shabaab , and said the assault had begun with suicide car bombs. The Somali federal government made a similar claim last month after Laftagaren’s forces launched another attack on Baidoa. Regional authorities and the federal government have yet to provide any tangible evidence for the assertion that the attackers were Al-Shabaab. The latest fighting left multiple people dead and caused other casualties, although there are no official figures. Among those killed was the commander of the personal guards of current Southwest leader Adan Madobe. Isaq Abdulle, commander of the Somali army’s 8th Brigade of the 60th Division, sustained serious injuries. Baidoa was once a relatively peaceful town under Laftagaren, but it has become a battleground since he was toppled. The repeated attacks by his forces have exposed the inability of the federal government and its Southwest allies to defend the city, even after thousands of troops were deployed there since March, analysts say. The latest assault highlights the continuing security crisis in Baidoa, where recurrent fighting has challenged the federal government’s control of the Southwest State capital. items.title: Red Cross helps 38,500 families reconnect as Sudan’s missing-person crisis deepens
items.summary: By Suleiman Siri for Radio Dabanga More than 11,000 people are now registered as missing... The post Red Cross helps 38,500 families reconnect as Sudan’s missing-person crisis deepens appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: By Suleiman Siri for Radio Dabanga More than 11,000 people are now registered as missing in Sudan, a 40% increase in the past year, as the war fuels displacement, arrests, and disappearances, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). The ICRC has helped 38,512 families reconnect or maintain contact with relatives, while clarifying the fate and whereabouts of 613 missing people in the first half of 2026, its spokesperson in Sudan, Farid Al Humaid, told Radio Dabanga. Farid El Humaid, spokesperson for the ICRC delegation in Sudan (Photo: Supplied / ICRC) The issue of people who have disappeared or gone missing is no longer simply a matter of figures in human rights and media reports. It has become a grave concern for families, communities, and international and local organisations as disappearances become increasingly common as the war spreads. The crisis has worsened amid waves of displacement, as civilians flee fighting between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). After battles end, campaigns of arrests often follow, with people accused of political or ethnic affiliation. In many cases, relatives are denied information about detainees, leaving families in a cycle of anguish, uncertainty, and psychological distress. Organisations searching for missing people face major obstacles, including a lack of coordination and the absence of a central database recording people who have disappeared or gone missing. The absence of legislation criminalising enforced disappearance has also contributed to the lack of specialised prosecution and courts. For international organisations such as the ICRC, access to detention facilities remains a major challenge. Disrupted communications networks in some areas, combined with the direct impact of the conflict, have further complicated field coordination. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) facilitated the release of 64 Sudanese army detainees who had been held captive by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) (File photo: ICRC) Field coordination Al Humaid says field coordination depends heavily on the ICRC’s partnership with the Sudanese Red Crescent Society, whose volunteers are present on the frontlines and are well placed to reach vulnerable communities and act as a link between the ICRC and the people it serves. “In the first half of 2026 alone, the ICRC and the Sudanese Red Crescent Society provided assistance to 1,973 people through telephone calls and field visits, including through the ICRC’s Restoring Family Links hotline,” he says. “In addition, we helped 38,512 families reconnect or maintain contact through our free telephone service.” Families searching for missing relatives can contact the ICRC, the Red Cross, or Red Crescent societies where they are based, or call the ICRC’s free Restoring Family Links hotline from inside Sudan on 60222, Al Humaid tells Radio Dabanga. In 2025, the ICRC clarified the fate and whereabouts of 846 missing people registered with it, providing their families with some reassurance and an end to the uncertainty they had endured. A child who fled with his family from El Fasher to Tawila shows signs of beatings and injuries (Photo: ICRC) During the first half of 2026, the ICRC also provided wireless internet services to 7,630 people and mobile phone charging services to 7,226, helping people maintain contact and avoid losing communication during emergencies. Preventing disappearances The only real guarantee against disappearances being repeated is strict adherence to international humanitarian law by all parties involved in hostilities, Al Humaid says. “We continue to urge all these parties to take every possible measure to prevent people from disappearing,” he says. This includes registering the identities of everyone who is detained or displaced, allowing detainees to communicate with their families, clarifying the fate of people who disappear, and ensuring that the remains of the dead are managed safely and with dignity. The ICRC says it maintains confidential and ongoing dialogue with authorities and armed actors to incorporate these obligations under international humanitarian law into their operational procedures. Al Humaid told Radio Dabanga that the ICRC’s biggest obstacles concern access to detention facilities, which is currently severely restricted. Disrupted communications networks in some areas and the direct impact of the conflict have made field coordination even more difficult. Despite the challenges, the ICRC continues to engage in bilateral and confidential dialogue with all parties to the conflict to seek safe, unimpeded, and sustained humanitarian access, including to detention facilities. Displaced people queue for aid in Darfur (File photo: Mohamed Jamal/ICRC) “In these discussions, we remind them of their obligations under international humanitarian law to respect minimum standards, ensure detainees can be traced, treat them with dignity, and meet their basic needs,” Al Humaid says. Missing or forcibly disappeared? There may be some overlap between detainees and victims of enforced disappearance, Al Humaid says. A family may consider a relative missing if they receive no information about their fate or whereabouts after the person has been arrested or detained. However, not every case of detention without notification necessarily constitutes enforced disappearance. The term has a specific legal meaning, and determining whether it applies requires an assessment of the individual circumstances of each case. Families regularly contact the ICRC about relatives they believe may have been arrested or detained. The organisation records these requests and, through confidential bilateral dialogue with the relevant authorities, seeks to establish the fate and whereabouts of the people concerned and, where possible, help restore contact with their families. As a neutral and independent humanitarian organisation, the ICRC does not publish detailed statistics on individual cases in which missing people are found in detention or dead during search efforts. “This confidential approach is essential,” Al Humaid says. “It enables us to secure access, search for missing people on behalf of their families, and ultimately obtain answers for them, without politicising the process or putting our access to vulnerable people at risk.” Three-part response The ICRC is carrying out a comprehensive response in close coordination with the Sudanese Red Crescent Society, centred on three areas: restoring contact, searching for missing people, and managing human remains. The organisation operates a Restoring Family Links hotline and provides direct services, including free telephone calls and Wi-Fi, to gather initial information and help families maintain or restore contact, particularly during emergencies such as displacement. ICRC teams and Sudanese Red Crescent volunteers collect requests to search for missing people and conduct searches on behalf of their families. The ICRC also supports relevant authorities and the Sudanese Red Crescent Society in managing human remains safely and with dignity. This includes distributing body bags, rehabilitating mortuaries, and training first responders and forensic workers in safe burial practices. Such measures are crucial for ensuring that people can be identified in the future, Al Humaid concludes. Relief agency with Sudanese refugees (File photo” Radio Dabanga) Note: This report has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. items.title: Air strike destroys WFP food aid trucks in Sudan’s Kordofan
items.summary: The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has condemned an aerial attack on two trucks carrying... The post Air strike destroys WFP food aid trucks in Sudan’s Kordofan appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: The UN World Food Programme (WFP) has condemned an aerial attack on two trucks carrying food aid to families in South Kordofan. A WFP statement on Wednesday confirms that the trucks were hit outside Dilling on 30 August while carrying WFP assistance to Kadugli. They were clearly marked with WFP banners and flags, WFP says. “More than 50 tonnes of food were destroyed, including cereals, yellow split peas, vegetable oil, and salt. The supplies were enough to provide life-saving assistance to 5,800 people for a month,” the WFP statement says. In Kadugli, the organisation is supporting nearly 58,000 people facing emergency levels of food insecurity or worse with food aid. The agency laments that the attack is the latest to disrupt the work of the WFP and other humanitarian agencies in Sudan. The agency says it has recorded eight aerial attacks since the beginning of the year that have damaged its premises and disrupted operations. The WFP has urged all parties involved in the fighting to respect international humanitarian law and protect civilians, humanitarian workers, and aid supplies. “Attacks on aid workers and humanitarian operations are unacceptable and must stop,” it says. items.title: Sudan’s Sovereignty Council chief inspects army's readiness in Blue Nile State amid escalating clashes with RSF
items.summary: Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's visit comes amid escalating clashes between army, Raid Support Forces in Blue Nile State
items.body:
The chairman of Sudan’s Sovereign Council, Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, inspected the readiness of the army on Wednesday in Blue Nile state in southeastern Sudan.

The visit comes amid escalating clashes in the state between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N).

In a statement, the army’s 4th infantry division said that Burhan, who also commands the Sudanese army, visited the city of Damazin, the state capital and the headquarters of the division.

It added that Burhan inspected the division’s forces and assessed their combat readiness and preparedness to carry out their assigned missions.

He was also briefed on the security and operational situation in the region, according to the statement.

Burhan stressed “the need to raise levels of preparedness and vigilance and strengthen discipline and combat readiness," according to the statement.

He also called for “continuing to carry out missions in accordance with military plans and directives."

Burhan also inspected the military hospital in Damazin, where he was briefed on the conditions of wounded soldiers and patients, and the hospital’s operations.

He affirmed the army command’s commitment to its personnel and to providing them with the necessary care.

The statement quoted 4th Infantry Division Commander Maj. Gen. Ismail al-Tayeb, who said Burhan’s visit “enhanced their readiness to carry out their missions.”

“The division’s forces are fully prepared to perform their military duties, secure the region and protect civilians,” he said.

He added that the division was ready to “continue implementing the plans and directives issued by the command.”

Burhan’s visit comes amid rapidly developing military developments in Blue Nile state.

On Tuesday, the first contingent of joint forces from armed movements allied with the army arrived in Blue Nile state.

On Saturday, the army announced that it deployed an elite brigade affiliated with the General Intelligence Service to the battlefield in the Bakori axis in the state.

The RSF announced Friday that it seized the Bakori and Sarkam military bases southeast of Damazin.

The army also announced last Thursday that it had shot down a “hostile” drone in Blue Nile state after it crossed the border from Ethiopia.

It said it was the third drone it had announced shooting down within a week.

In addition to Blue Nile and the Darfur region in western Sudan, clashes have been ongoing in the three Kordofan states -- North, West and South Kordofan -- between the army and the RSF since Oct. 25.

Sudan has been witnessing a war between the army and the RSF since April 2023, which has killed tens of thousands and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.title: Somalia: Armed militias seize election centers in Beledweyne
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Armed militias seized centers designated for voter registration in Beledweyne on Tuesday, as Somalia’s electoral commission set September 30 for Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections, intensifying opposition to the planned vote, Caasimada Online news website reported on Tuesday. Some of the militias, speaking to local media, said they oppose the elections b
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Armed militias seized centers designated for voter registration in Beledweyne on Tuesday, as Somalia’s electoral commission set September 30 for Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections, intensifying opposition to the planned vote, Caasimada Online news website reported on Tuesday. Some of the militias, speaking to local media, said they oppose the elections being conducted by the government-appointed electoral commission. They said they would not accept a vote in which only one favored candidate is allowed to contest while all other candidates are banned, arguing that the process mirrors such an arrangement. The Somali federal government has not yet taken any action against the militias. The seizure comes as Hawadle clan politicians strongly oppose the planned Hirshabelle election, saying the process is not fair. They are also demanding their turn at the presidency of the Hirshabelle regional administration. The competing objections have placed the planned elections under heightened political tension in Beledweyne, where the seizure of the registration centers has directly disrupted locations designated for the electoral process. The militias’ opposition centers on what they describe as a process that favors one candidate while excluding others, while Hawadle politicians are challenging the fairness of the Hirshabelle election and pressing for their turn at the regional presidency. With the electoral commission having scheduled the Hirshabelle municipal and parliamentary elections for September 30, the dispute over the process remains unresolved, while the Somali federal government has yet to take action against the militias. items.title: Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC
items.summary: Since at least 2025, hundreds of schoolchildren have been denied access to schools and educational facilities due to the violent clashes between the rebel groups and state forces. The resurgence of the Ebola virus has worsened the situation, as schools tried to reopen amid the disease outbreak. The post Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: Violent clashes between the Congolese armed forces and the M23 rebels have disrupted school reopenings in several localities in North Kivu in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). As the 2026-2027 academic year begins, schools have not yet reopened in several rural areas of the region, particularly in the Bankindi, Banamulema, and Balindu communities of the Kisimba tribal group. Just before the school year was set to begin, many families were forced to flee their homes to escape the intense fighting between the armed groups, particularly the Wazalendo militia, and the M23/AFC rebels in the region. Parents, students, and teachers have sought refuge to avoid the crossfire. Some families have taken shelter in the bushes, while others have relocated to towns like Pinga and Kalembe. The situation is severely compromising the normal reopening of school activities. For the displaced families, the immediate priority is survival, especially since they lack the means to pay school fees for their children. “We escaped with our children without carrying along our belongings. Today, we do not even know where we will sleep or what we will eat,” a parent taking refuge with his family in Pinga told HumAngle. “Under these conditions, it is difficult for us to think about school fees, uniforms or other school needs for our children. We very much wish for peace to return so that our children can return to school.” Some schools in Pinga have started admitting children of displaced families from zones affected by the fighting. A senior official from Kabeza Secondary School in Pinga, whose name is withheld for safety reasons, stated that the influx of students creates space issues, as the school must accommodate additional students from war-affected areas. “We are forced to welcome children from displaced families in order to enable them to continue their education. However, admitting them is not easy because some come without school requirements and their parents do not have the means to meet their needs. We demand assistance so that these children are not abandoned because of the war,” the official said. Faced with this situation, authorities in the education sector of the Walikale 3 sub-division are encouraging displaced parents to enrol their children in schools in their refuge zones, notably in Pinga and Kalembe, so they can continue schooling. Families hiding in bushes with their children, lacking access to schools, subsistence means, and essential services, are compromising their children’s educational futures. Since at least 2025, hundreds of schoolchildren have been denied access to schools and educational facilities due to the violent clashes between the rebel groups and state forces. The resurgence of the Ebola virus has worsened the situation, as schools tried to reopen amid the disease outbreak. The post Violent Clashes Stall School Reopenings in DRC appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria
items.summary: The surge in kidnapping near Cameroon’s border with Nigeria coincides with several ongoing crises in the region. The post Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: A report from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (UNOCHA) has revealed that over 300 persons were kidnapped by terrorists in the Far North region of Cameroon during April, May, and June of 2026. In the same timeframe in 2025, 141 abductions were reported, which is a staggering 118 per cent increase in kidnappings. The recent report shows a serious decline in the region’s security landscape in the second quarter of 2026. During this period, 72 people were killed, and 48 were injured, which actually reflects a 6.5 per cent decrease in fatalities compared to the previous year, when 77 civilians lost their lives. The UNOCHA report stresses that understanding the worsening security situation in Far North Cameroon requires more than just looking at casualty numbers. Compared to the latter half of 2025, there were 167 more kidnappings, suggesting that abductions have become the major form of violence affecting communities near the Nigerian border. Beyond the loss of lives, terrorist operations in the region seem to have established a pervasive climate of fear, limiting movement and undermining the livelihood of local communities. The report states that such violence can lead to new displacements as people flee to areas deemed safer. For humanitarian organisations, the ongoing insecurity complicates efforts to deliver assistance to those in need. The report also noted a resurgence of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) in the Logone-et-Chari division, with two such incidents occurring between April and June this year. While the limited occurrences of IEDs do not definitively indicate a sustained reduction in violence, they add to the potential risks faced by residents and humanitarian workers, especially during periods of displacement in violence-affected areas. This surge in kidnappings coincides with several ongoing crises in the region. The UNOCHA report mentions new population displacements, a worsening measles outbreak, the emergence of cholera cases, and ongoing food insecurity. The post Kidnapping on the Rise Near Cameroon’s Border with Nigeria appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Displaced people in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan face humanitarian and health catastrophe
items.summary: About 6,200 children are suffering from malnutrition in Malha in North Darfur, while a cholera... The post Displaced people in Sudan’s Darfur and Kordofan face humanitarian and health catastrophe appeared first on Dabanga Radio TV Online .
items.body: About 6,200 children are suffering from malnutrition in Malha in North Darfur, while a cholera outbreak is causing a health crisis in Um Jak administrative area and the Hamir Um Taqola village in West Kordofan, the General Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugee Camps and the Dar Hamar Emergency Room say. Adam Rijal, the official spokesperson for the coordination, says in a statement on Tuesday that about 6,200 children in Malha are malnourished, including around 1,500 suffering from severe acute malnutrition. About 1,350 pregnant and breastfeeding women are also malnourished, he says. Several diseases, including tuberculosis, anaemia, and diarrhoea, are widespread in the locality, Rijal says, while medicines are available only in very limited quantities and humanitarian organisations are completely absent from the area. He describes the humanitarian and health situation in Malha as catastrophic and forgotten by the world, and calls on the United Nations and international organisations to break the isolation imposed on Malha, send emergency teams, and open an independent international investigation into the violations that have led to the humanitarian collapse. In West Kordofan, the Dar Hamar Emergency Room expresses concern about the catastrophic health situation in Um Jak administrative area and Hamir Um Taqola village, in the rural El Odaya Zakaria area and neighbouring villages, following a severe cholera outbreak. The emergency room says in a statement on Tuesday that eight people have died and 40 cases have been recorded over the past 48 hours. A spokesperson for the emergency room told Radio Dabanga that the area has no medical staff and no life-saving medicines or intravenous fluids. There are also no health isolation centres capable of containing the outbreak, the spokesperson says. Humanitarians step up cholera response amid conflict, rising needs OCHA reports that despite active conflict and funding shortfalls, humanitarian organizations continue to deliver life-saving assistance across Sudan. From January to July, the UN and humanitarian partners reached 12.3 million people across Sudan with at least one form of assistance. However, just 2.2 million people – or 18 per cent of those reached – received assistance across multiple sectors, underscoring the impact of underfunding and other challenges on efforts to reach people with the full range of support they need. Meanwhile, the UN and partners are stepping up efforts to tackle cholera as the rainy season continues. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), over 2,600 cases had been reported by early August across multiple states, with the Kordofan region at the epicentre. Health workers continue to provide treatment, conduct vaccination campaigns and distribute essential medical supplies. Tragically,WHO reports that a vaccinator was killed in an attack on a market in West Kordofan State on Saturday, while searching for her son among casualties from an earlier attack. Meanwhile, humanitarians are scaling up efforts to provide clean water. In Kordofan State, a water system rehabilitated with UNICEF support in Abu Jubayhah is now providing safe water to 25,000 people every day, including 5,000 displaced people. At the same time, insecurity continues to drive displacement, including in the Kordofan region. IOM reports that some 730 people fled several villages in Abassiya locality, South Kordofan, on Sunday. They sought safety elsewhere in Abassiya and in Um Rawaba locality in neighbouring North Kordofan. OCHA once again calls on all parties to protect civilians, including health and humanitarian workers, and to facilitate rapid, safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access. Note: This article has been translated from Arabic with the assistance of artificial intelligence tools, and subsequently reviewed and adapted by a human editor before publication. items.title: Somalia NSA confirms troops crossed into Ethiopia region
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Aways Haji Yusuf, on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that an undisclosed number of Somali National Army (SNA) troops who recently completed a Saudi Arabia-funded training program in Hanaanbure, Galmudug, have crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region. Yusuf said the soldiers, who had undergone more than a year […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – Somalia’s National Security Adviser, Aways Haji Yusuf, on Tuesday confirmed for the first time that an undisclosed number of Somali National Army (SNA) troops who recently completed a Saudi Arabia-funded training program in Hanaanbure, Galmudug, have crossed into Ethiopia’s Somali region. Yusuf said the soldiers, who had undergone more than a year of training, were granted leave to visit their families and that the federal government is aware of their presence in the region for that purpose. “If there are other issues, we will let you (media) know,” Yusuf told reporters. Defection Reports Preceded the Admission The confirmation comes days after multiple Somali media outlets, including outlets based in Ethiopia’s Somali region, reported that dozens of soldiers – part of a cohort of 3,000 trained at Hananbure – had defected and were subsequently captured by regional forces before being taken to Jigjiga. Reported figures for the number involved have varied widely across outlets, with some citing 300, others 180, and others as high as 900. None of these figures has been independently confirmed, and it remains unclear whether the soldiers defected or were simply on approved leave to visit their families, as the government maintains. Analyst: Admission “Likely to Generate More Questions” A Nairobi-based Horn of Africa analyst with Sahan Research described the National Security Adviser’s admission as “refreshing and commendable, but likely to generate more questions.” “Did Somalia recruit forces from the Somali Regional State of Ethiopia with permission from regional and federal authorities? If not, how will Addis Ababa respond?” the analyst asked. A Backdrop of Strained Ties The episode unfolds against a backdrop of strained relations between Mogadishu and Addis Ababa in recent years, with the two governments aligned to separate geopolitical camps. Ethiopia has increasingly sided with the United Arab Emirates, including in its support for the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, while Somalia has increasingly aligned itself with Saudi Arabia and Turkey. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.title: 22,000 displaced by fighting in Sudan’s Blue Nile state in last week: UN
items.summary: Agency says civilians fleeing violence in Geissan district have sought safety in several areas, including state capital Ed Damazine
items.body:
About 22,000 people have been displaced from Sudan’s Blue Nile state in the last week as fighting intensified in the Geissan district, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Tuesday.

OCHA said in a statement that continued violence is putting civilians at risk and forcing thousands to flee their homes.

“In Blue Nile State, local authorities report that nearly 22,000 people may have been displaced in the past seven days due to escalating fighting in the locality of Geissan,” it said.

The statement said that “many are sheltering in schools or have fled to other areas, including towards the state capital, Ed Damazine.”

The Geissan Emergency Room, a local aid body, said Sunday that nearly 20,000 people had fled the area of Medina 12 in the Geissan district because of the fighting and worsening security conditions.

Blue Nile has seen a new escalation in the last two days after the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North launched attacks in several areas of the state.

OCHA also said attacks on Saturday on villages north and northwest of El Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, caused casualties and displaced civilians, amid reports that civilian property and livestock were looted.

“In West Darfur State, civilians were reportedly killed and injured when a drone strike hit a fuel market in Adekong, near the border with Chad, last Thursday. The attack also damaged civilian property,” it said.

OCHA renewed its demand for all parties to the conflict “to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, respect international humanitarian law, and allow humanitarian organizations to operate safely and independently.”

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Monday that 450 people were displaced from the village of al-Qardud Abu Zeid in the al-Rahad district of North Kordofan because of deteriorating security in a single day.

Alongside Blue Nile and Darfur, fighting has continued since Oct. 25 in Sudan’s three Kordofan states -- North Kordofan, West Kordofan and South Kordofan -- between the army and the RSF.

Sudan has been at war between the army and the RSF since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced about 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.title: Terrorism forces 57 primary schools to shut in Nigeria’s Borno, 80 students remain captive: Official
items.summary: Soldiers have been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes.
items.body:
At least 57 primary schools are currently not functioning in Nigeria’s northeastern Borno State due to insecurity, while about 80 students abducted during attacks on schools remain in captivity, according to local education authorities.

The situation was disclosed by Fasuma Askira, education secretary of Askira-Uba Local Government Area, where only 56 of the 113 primary schools are currently operating.

On May 15, terrorists attacked Mussa Central Primary School and abducted dozens of children. Although the exact number remains disputed, the Borno State Government has more recently put the number of missing pupils at about 44.

On June 29, insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were sitting for a National Examinations Council examination. Some students were subsequently rescued, but 36 students and a teacher remained in captivity.

Combining the latest government estimate from Mussa with the verified Lassa figure puts the number of students still in captivity at about 80.

As of Aug. 31, the children abducted from Mussa had spent 108 days in captivity, while the Lassa students had been held for 63 days.

Simon Waindu, whose daughter is among the Lassa students, said none of the children had returned and that families had received no information about their rescue.

Meanwhile, authorities have closed schools in communities affected by insecurity. Authorities have also proposed the deployment of community vigilantes around schools when classes resume, while soldiers have been deployed in Mussa and Lassa alongside local vigilantes.

The latest developments come after Anadolu reported in June that terrorists abducted six women and two babies near the scene of a school attack in Borno state.

The incident occurred shortly after suspected insurgents attacked Government Day Secondary School in Lassa while students were taking examinations, further highlighting the vulnerability of civilians around schools in the conflict-affected region.

Nigeria's northeastern states have faced more than a decade of insurgency, with Boko Haram and ISWAP among the armed groups responsible for attacks, abductions and displacement.

The continued captivity of students and closure of schools raise concerns over the long-term educational consequences of the conflict, particularly for children in communities already affected by displacement and poverty.

items.title: Displacement and the Right to Vote: Addressing the Exclusion of Nigeria’s IDPs in the 2027 GeneralElections

items.body: Introduction Between April 2025 and June 2026, over 2.3 million internally displaced people (IDPs) were identified by the International Organisation for Migration’s 51st DTM Site Assessment. The data highlights a 2% increase from Round 50 of the assessment. The number represents a population of Nigerians covered by the constitution and, specifically, the National Policy on IDPs to restore their rights, agency and dignity. Mostly uprooted by long-running conflicts, HumAngle found that IDPs across various communities are being pushed outside the map of the 2027 electoral processes, denying them the opportunity to exercise their rights and exposing systemic failure and neglect. What’s New? HumAngle travelled to rural communities and town centres where IDPs are hosted. Across communities in Adamawa, Borno and Katsina states, there is a pattern of recurring barriers to IDPs’ electoral participation . These include incomplete voter registration exercises, difficulty replacing or transferring Permanent Voter Cards (PVCs), limited voter education, lack of information about registration procedures, the cost and insecurity associated with travelling to original polling units, and declining confidence in the electoral process. Key findings HumAngle identifies a policy gap in the management of IDP challenges. The National Policy on IDPs says all rights contained in the Nigerian constitution and humanitarian instruments are to be enjoyed by IDPs. Yet, this has not been the case across many IDP camps. There are practical barriers to voter registration. Often, due to logistical failure to reach IDP camps and the poor implementation of the Independent National Electoral Commission’s IDPs Voting Regulations . IDPs have demonstrated their desire for inclusion and participation in electoral processes, with many first-time voters hoping to be enrolled in the voter register. Voter education and information gaps in IDP communities persist. IDPs with lost or damaged voter cards do not know how to get a replacement, while INEC’s online self-service option is ineffective due to the digital gaps in IDP and conflict-affected communities. No polling infrastructure within IDP camps. Where field visits were conducted, IDPs who have their voter cards have to go back to communities they fled to vote, further exposing them to the risks of harm. Why does it matter? Inclusion is crucial for a constitutional democracy and a nation attempting to heal from radicalisation. In this context, it restores confidence in the state and gives agency to citizens who are in their most vulnerable state. Invariably, this enhances recovery, and restores a sense of belonging for a population that seems to exist in limbo. Social recovery does not work in isolation. It has to be a whole approach, and INEC’s voter registration and participation in elections by IDPs is part of this larger process of recovery and agency-giving for IDPs. The integrity of electoral processes is only intact when no one feels excluded. What can be done INEC should create a special window urgently to regularise IDPs, register those of voting age with a special target to first-time voters across identified communities. This will enable the completion of registration, enrolment of new voters, and replacement of lost or damaged cards ahead of the 2027 elections. INEC should revamp its voter education campaign through collaboration with the National Orientation Agency and Local Government Community Development Departments to reach IDPs with clear and needed voter education and information. Civil society and the media should continue independent monitoring and reporting on voter registration and election-related exercises to keep issues visible to policymakers and the public. Humanitarian and camp management actors should integrate voter education activities within camp programmes to bridge awareness gaps. They should also leverage existing camp leadership structures to coordinate with INEC, schedule visits and follow up. The National Commission for Refugees, Migrants and Internally Displaced Persons (NCFRMI) should review the National IDP Policy and develop a complementary national framework that elaborately operationalises how the participation of IDPs in elections should henceforth be governed. Conclusion The 2027 general election is near, and IDPs, especially first-time voters, are enthusiastic and hopeful to participate in a civic exercise. The constitution granted them the right; the laws and policies empower them with the opportunity, but the system is locking them out. This clash between policy and practice has consequences. It disenfranchises and breeds national grievances where healing, recovery and agency should take centre. INEC and all relevant stakeholders have a role to reverse the dying hope for inclusion, stronger democracy and electoral integrity. Further reading Nigeria’s Displaced Communities Risk Being Shut Out of Elections, https://www.humanglemedia.com/nigerias-displaced-communities-risk-being-shut-out-of-elections Regulations for Voting by Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), https://www.inecnigeria.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/REGULATIONS.pdf Acknowledgment This policy brief was made possible through the dedication of a talented team of professionals, led by Abdussamad Ahmad Yusuf, for the research, analysis, and drafting of this document. The post Displacement and the Right to Vote: Addressing the Exclusion of Nigeria’s IDPs in the 2027 GeneralElections appeared first on HumAngle .

items.title: Italy Expands Police Training Support for Somalia
items.summary: Talyaaniga ayaa Muqdisho ku shaaciyay qorshe lagu xoojinayo iskaashiga amni ee Soomaaliya, iyadoo diiradda la saarayo tababarka booliiska, dhismaha hay’adaha amniga iyo ka hortagga xagjirnimada. The post Italy Expands Police Training Support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .
items.body: Italy expands police training and security support for Somalia Italian Ambassador Pier Mario Daccò Coppi says Rome will deepen its cooperation with Somalia on police training, institutional development and efforts to prevent violent extremism. MOGADISHU, September 1, 2026 — Italy has pledged to strengthen its support for Somalia’s security institutions, with an emphasis on police training, stabilisation and government-led projects in communities affected by conflict.Speaking at Somalia’s National Internal Security Conference in Mogadishu, Italian Ambassador Pier Mario Daccò Coppi described the gathering as an important opportunity to bring together the political and institutional leadership of the internal security sector The two-day conference brings together representatives of the federal government and federal member states to discuss security governance, institutional coordination and the supervisory role of the Ministry of Internal Security.Daccò Coppi said Somalia was making important progress in institution-building and stabilisation, although the process remained gradual. Longstanding police and security cooperation The ambassador described relations between Italy and Somalia as a historic partnership that had endured the instability and conflict of Somalia’s recent past. He said Italy’s policy was guided by support for Somalia’s sovereignty, territorial integrity, security and stabilisation. The two countries have maintained a defence cooperation framework since 2013. The Italian Carabinieri began training members of the Somali Police Force’s Darwish units in Djibouti in 2014. According to the Italian Ministry of Defence, the MIADIT programme trained 3,100 Somali police personnel over its first 10 years. The courses cover law enforcement, stability policing and responses to high-risk security incidents. Italian Ministry of Defence Italy also participates in three European Union operations linked to Somalia: EUTM Somalia, EUCAP Somalia and Operation Atalanta.EUTM supports military training, EUCAP helps strengthen civilian law-enforcement capacity, and Atalanta focuses on maritime security and counter-piracy operations. Five-year police training framework Daccò Coppi highlighted a memorandum signed in Mogadishu on July 3, 2026, by Somali Internal Security Minister Abdullahi Sheikh Ismail Fartag and Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi.The memorandum creates a government-to-government framework for vocational and academic police training, train-the-trainer programmes, study visits, exchanges and the sharing of professional expertise.It also establishes a joint working group responsible for coordinating implementation, reviewing progress and planning future activities.The framework will remain in force for an initial five years and may be renewed through the written consent of both governments. Somalia’s Ministry of Internal Security The ambassador said a further agreement on police training was expected to follow. He added that broader cooperation between the two countries’ police institutions would support efforts against transnational organised crime, irregular migration and terrorism. No date or detailed terms for the expected follow-up agreement were announced. Preventing violent extremism Daccò Coppi argued that force and legislation alone were not sufficient to counter violent extremism.He said security measures should be accompanied by efforts to address social and economic conditions that can contribute to radicalisation.The ambassador connected this approach to the Towards Peace and Stability in Somalia , or TPSS, programme launched by Italy and the Federal Government of Somalia.Under the initiative, Somali authorities identify priority interventions, while Italy provides funding for projects intended to strengthen services and stability in vulnerable areas. Health projects in three districts Somalia’s Office of the Prime Minister selected health projects in three districts: Afmadow in Jubaland Harardhere in Galmudug Adale in Hirshabeelle In Adale, the programme will rehabilitate and bring Sheikh Ahmed Gabyow Hospital into operation. The district has a population of approximately 100,000 people, including internally displaced communities.The TPSS programme has an initial budget of €3.82 million. It is financed by Italy and implemented by the Somali Prime Minister’s Office. Italian Agency for Development Cooperation Daccò Coppi said he hoped the conference would strengthen institutional coordination and improve the capabilities of Somalia’s security forces.He said the long-term objective was for Somali institutions to assume full responsibility for national security through the lawful, legitimate and accountable use of force. The post Italy Expands Police Training Support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .

items.title: Türkiye pledges continued security and economic support for Somalia
items.summary: Danjiraha Turkiga Alper Aktaş oo ka hadlaya Shirweynaha Qaran ee Amniga Gudaha ee Muqdisho The post Türkiye pledges continued security and economic support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .
items.body: Turkish Ambassador Alper Aktaş says Ankara will maintain its support for Somali security forces while expanding cooperation in energy, fisheries and other strategic sectors. MOGADISHU, September 1, 2026 — Türkiye has pledged to continue supporting Somalia’s security institutions, counterterrorism operations and long-term economic development as the country works towards greater self-sufficiency.Addressing Somalia’s National Internal Security Conference in Mogadishu, Turkish Ambassador Alper Aktaş said the country had made visible security progress, although significant challenges and uncertainties remained.Aktaş said his more than two and a half years in Somalia had allowed him to witness changes in Mogadishu firsthand. “Just a few years ago, Mogadishu was associated with major explosions, instability and persistent conflict,” he said. “Today, we speak of rising skyscrapers, ambitious development projects and genuine hope.” Training for Gorgor and Haramcad units The ambassador said Türkiye-trained Gorgor special forces continued to take part in operations against terrorist groups.He added that Türkiye was also training specialised Haramcad units within the Somali Police Force.According to Aktaş, more than 1,000 personnel have been trained and are helping respond to security threats in Somali cities. He did not provide a breakdown of the personnel, the period covered by the figure or their current deployments.Türkiye opened its largest overseas military base in Mogadishu in 2017 and provides training to both the Somali military and police. Air support for security operations Aktaş said Türkiye had increased its air assets in Somalia at the request of Somali authorities to support operations on the ground.He said the additional support was already contributing to counterterrorism efforts. However, he did not identify the aircraft involved, disclose their number or provide independently verifiable information about their operational impact.Further information from the Somali and Turkish authorities would therefore be needed to establish the scope and results of the deployment. Connecting security with economic development The ambassador argued that security gains would not be sustainable without economic progress. He linked Türkiye’s security engagement to its growing involvement in Somalia’s energy, fisheries and infrastructure sectors.Aktaş referred to the continuing work of the Çağrı Bey deep-sea drilling vessel, planned fisheries initiatives and a proposed spaceport project.The Çağrı Bey arrived off Mogadishu in April 2026 to begin Türkiye’s first overseas deep-sea oil exploration project. The planned well is expected to reach a depth of 7,500 metres, while the drilling operation was projected to last about 10 months.The operation follows an intergovernmental energy agreement signed in March 2024 covering the exploration, evaluation, development and production of oil and gas in Somalia’s offshore and onshore areas. Exploratory drilling does not, however, guarantee the discovery of commercially recoverable oil. The results of the well, the possible size of any reserves and the eventual financial benefits for Somalia have not yet been announced. Commitment to continued partnership Aktaş said international partners should maintain their assistance as Somalia moves towards greater self-reliance. “Türkiye remains fully committed to doing its part,” he said. He concluded by thanking Somalia’s security institutions and described the country as a second home for himself and his family.His remarks presented Türkiye’s engagement as a broad partnership spanning security, defence, energy and economic development. Some proposed initiatives, particularly the spaceport, still require further official details concerning financing, implementation agreements and timelines. The post Türkiye pledges continued security and economic support for Somalia first appeared on Radio Dalsan .

items.title: Somalia Sets September 30 for Galmudug, Hirshabelle Elections
items.summary: The elections hold broader significance for Somalia's political stability. Any delays or disputes could undermine progress toward the national elections scheduled for 2027. Both elections will proceed simul
items.body: Electoral commission announces fresh polls for two federal member states following court ruling that annulled Galmudug’s previous results. Mogadishu – Somalia’s Independent National Electoral and Boundaries Commission has scheduled September 30, 2026, as polling day for local council and parliamentary elections in Galmudug and Hirshabelle. The commission released separate electoral timelines for both federal member states on Tuesday, marking a significant step toward completing the country’s ongoing regional election process. The decision comes after Somalia’s Supreme Court annulled Galmudug’s previous election results on August 23, citing irregularities in the electoral process. This ruling forced the federal member state to conduct fresh polls, adding pressure on the electoral commission to deliver credible and transparent elections within a compressed timeframe. Hirshabelle, meanwhile, will proceed with its scheduled elections as originally planned. Galmudug’s electoral calendar begins on September 10, when the commission will designate polling centers and voting stations. Political associations must submit their candidate lists by September 20, followed by the accreditation of party agents and observers on September 26. The shortened timeline reflects the urgency of completing the process after the court’s intervention. Campaign activities will conclude on September 28, two days before polling day. Hirshabelle’s electoral process started earlier, with the publication of a preliminary voter register on September 2. The commission will subsequently establish polling stations, register voters, distribute voter cards, and verify candidate lists. Political associations will announce their candidates on September 22, followed by the accreditation of party agents and observers. Campaigning will end on September 28. “These elections represent an important opportunity for citizens in Galmudug and Hirshabelle to exercise their democratic rights,” a senior electoral official told this reporter on condition of anonymity. The official emphasized the commission’s commitment to transparency and fairness. The elections hold broader significance for Somalia’s political stability. Federal member state elections are crucial for establishing legitimate regional administrations that can partner with the federal government on security, development, and constitutional reform. Any delays or disputes could undermine progress toward the national elections scheduled for 2027. Both elections will proceed simultaneously on September 30, with results expected shortly thereafter.
