items.title: Al-Shabaab-Houthi alliance poses a new threat to the U.S. and its allies
items.summary: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – On a balmy evening, Jibril “One-Armed” Yahya Ali and his new bride set out for a honeymoon drive along the beach outside al-Ghaydah, Yemen. Jibril, a Somali, and his Yemeni wife had met through a mutual acquaintance, an arms dealer who helped Jibril buy military-grade weapons from Yemen’s Houthi rebels. Jibril would then […]
items.body: MOGADISHU (Somaliguardian) – On a balmy evening, Jibril “One-Armed” Yahya Ali and his new bride set out for a honeymoon drive along the beach outside al-Ghaydah, Yemen . Jibril, a Somali, and his Yemeni wife had met through a mutual acquaintance, an arms dealer who helped Jibril buy military-grade weapons from Yemen ’s Houthi rebels. Jibril would then smuggle the arms to al-Shabaab, an Islamist insurgent group fighting to overthrow the government in Somalia. The budding alliance benefited both sides. Al-Shabaab, the world’s richest al Qaeda wing, had cash but needed weapons and training. The Houthis had sophisticated arms and tech know-how, but coveted money and a new perch for attacks against the West. The exchange also made Jibril a target . On Feb. 12, four months after Jibril married Budoor Murshid, the couple took the Toyota Corolla on their sunset drive. Budoor’s phone rang. They parked, and Budoor stepped outside to take the call. Moments later, a U.S. missile slammed through the car roof. Rather than explode, it sliced up the Corolla like a weaponized can opener. Jibril died instantly. A friend spirited Budoor away. The airstrike was an opening shot in the American effort to disrupt the unlikely alliance between two implacable U.S. foes: al-Shabaab militants who have been fighting in Somalia for two decades, and the Houthi rebels, longtime beneficiaries of weapons and training from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. For the U.S., Jibril’s death came too late to stop the chain of events he helped set in motion. The Houthis and al-Shabaab had been sectarian adversaries until Jibril and others brokered a partnership that now threatens to further destabilize the Middle East and energy markets worldwide. Their home countries, Yemen and Somalia, sit on opposite shores of the Gulf of Aden , through which 12% of the world’s seaborne oil passed before the Iran war. With the Strait of Hormuz all but closed by Iranian forces, the gulf could serve as an escape route for Middle East oil. Except the Houthis have come to the aid of their allies in Tehran, attacking Saudi-linked oil tankers with missiles and drones in the Red Sea. Since at least 2023, Jibril had served as a liaison between the two militant groups, united in their hatred of America and Israel, according to U.S., Somali and Yemeni officials. Jibril was killed two weeks before the U.S. began the war with Iran. He never saw his legacy—how two U.S.-designated terrorist groups, locked in a marriage of convenience, inherited a strategic maritime pinch-point that empowers them to threaten the global oil trade in a time of crisis. “You have al-Shabaab, al Qaeda’s largest and most lucrative affiliate, gaining access to more sophisticated weapons and training,” U.S. Gen. Dagvin Anderson, commander of American forces in Africa, told The Wall Street Journal. “On the other side, the Houthis are extending their geographic reach, gaining a foothold that could further destabilize one of the world’s most critical economic chokepoints,” he said. “This isn’t just a regional problem. It has global implications.” Two American sources familiar with the operation confirmed it was a U.S. airstrike that killed Jibril. U.S. Central Command, in charge of American forces in the Middle East, said it wasn’t a military operation. A Central Intelligence Agency spokesperson declined to say whether the spy service was behind the killing. Yemen’s ambassador to the U.S. declined an interview request. Houthi officials didn’t respond to written questions about the group’s relationship with al-Shabaab. Budoor couldn’t be reached for comment. Enemy of my enemy The Houthis, predominantly Shia Muslims, and al-Shabaab, which adheres to Sunni Islam, are among the hundreds of millions divided by a seventh-century schism over who was the rightful successor to the Prophet Muhammad. The sectarian split still flares into violence in spots from Afghanistan to Iraq to Syria. Common enemies, however, now unite the Houthis and al-Shabaab. “They hate the West, they hate Israel,” said Abdulaahi Mohamed Ali, a former Somali intelligence chief. Yemen’s Counter-Terrorism Service described Jibril as “one of the key figures in strengthening ties between the Houthis and al-Shabaab through the exchange of expertise and coordination, particularly in facilitating the transfer of weapons and military equipment,” according to an internal assessment reviewed by the Journal. Jibril moved clandestinely between Somalia and Yemen, operating as al-Shabaab’s liaison with Houthi command, according to Matt Bryden, a former United Nations official who monitored arms flows to Somalia. Bryden outlined Jibril’s life and death in a closed-door intelligence briefing in June attended by U.S. special-operations personnel and East African government officials. Jibril, 38 years old when he died, had studied veterinary medicine in Yemen and ran a charity in Mogadishu, Somalia’s capital. He owned a foreign-exchange outlet and an import-export firm. He bore scars from gunshot wounds. His injuries earned him the nickname Gacaamey—roughly translated as one-armed—despite his having both limbs. The Houthis provided Jibril with a furnished apartment in San’a, the rebel-controlled Yemeni capital, according to the briefing, and he attended official functions. The rebels issued him a phony but convincing Yemeni passport under an assumed name, according to a document viewed by the Journal. In 2024, al-Shabaab dispatched a more senior envoy, Sheikh Ahmed Elmi Samatar, to work alongside Jibril. Samatar presented the Houthis with a lengthy weapons wish list, viewed by the Journal, which included shoulder-fired antiaircraft missiles, 107 mm Katyusha rockets, Dragunov sniper rifles, explosive attack drones, antitank missiles and U.S. night-vision gear. A U.S. military intelligence official confirmed that al-Shabaab sought advanced weaponry from the Houthis, in addition to rifles, machine guns and ammunition. Yemeni government officials arrested Samatar in January 2025 and later released him in a prisoner exchange with the Houthis, according to the briefing. Samatar returned to Somalia, leaving Jibril to press al-Shabaab’s interests in Yemen. Jibril continued to broker arms shipments, and al-Shabaab dispatched two weapons experts to Yemen to assist him. After Jibril’s killing, al-Shabaab picked a replacement in Yemen to continue the work, Bryden said. Jibril’s wife is on the run, he said. Front companies in Yemen disguise the shipments as civilian products and move them to Mukalla and other ports, the Yemeni intelligence report said. The weapons cross the Gulf of Aden in speedboats or fishing vessels and are transferred ashore on poorly monitored sections of coastline in northern Somalia, according to the U.S. military-intelligence official. They are transported to al-Shabaab combat units in southern Somalia, where the insurgents’ activities are concentrated. In April 2025, the U.S. destroyed two unflagged boats entering Somali waters from Yemen, carrying what U.S. Africa Command described as advanced conventional weapons. It isn’t clear what items on the lengthy al-Shabaab wish list have reached the militants in Somalia. But the idea that al-Shabaab might acquire attack drones or other arms capable of striking U.S. and Somali bases from the air makes both militaries nervous. “I don’t know what their plans are, but there’s definitely something cooking,” said Brig. Gen. Ahmed Abdullahi Sheikh, a former commander of Somali special forces. Complicating security concerns was Israel’s decision in December to recognize the independence of Somaliland, a region within the northwest of Somalia’s acknowledged borders that declared itself a separate country in 1991. Somaliland could provide Israel access to Berbera, a Red Sea port city with a runway so long that NASA once rented it as an emergency landing strip for the space shuttle. Berbera could give the Israelis another position where they could monitor and attack their Houthi enemies. Michael Milshtein, a former senior Israeli intelligence officer, said the Houthis were front of mind when Israel recognized Somaliland as an independent nation. “Military deployment in Somaliland gives you a very strong position to confront the Houthis,” he said. The Israeli government didn’t respond to requests for comment. In a televised speech this month, Houthi leader Abdul Malik al-Houthi said the group was closely monitoring Israeli actions in Somaliland, which he alleged were aimed at controlling the Gulf of Aden, the Bab al-Mandeb strait and the Red Sea. “We will move at any time to target any activity or presence of the Israeli enemy in Somaliland,” al-Houthi said. Traffic stop In June, a four-person Houthi delegation set sail from Yemen, crossed the Gulf of Aden and came ashore in southern Somalia. The men trekked through the bush to meet with their counterparts in Jilib, the de facto capital of al-Shabaab-held territory, according

items.title: SNA brobes video of soldiers suffocating bound Al-Shabaab suspect
items.summary: Somalia’s military opened a preliminary investigation on Tuesday after a video circulated online appeared to show members of the Somali National Army (SNA) abusing a man in custody during an operation against Al-Shabaab, the SNAF Command said in a statement, adding that the footage contravenes its Code of Conduct and the laws of armed conflict. items.body: Somalia’s military opened a preliminary investigation on Tuesday after a video circulated online appeared to show members of the Somali National Army (SNA) abusing a man in custody during an operation against Al-Shabaab, the SNAF Command said in a statement, adding that the footage contravenes its Code of Conduct and the laws of armed conflict. The probe lands at a sensitive moment for Somalia’s armed forces, which are locked in an intensifying offensive against Al-Shabaab across multiple regions. Any confirmed breach of prisoner-of-war protections could complicate ties with international partners who fund and train SNAF units, and would test the military’s willingness to discipline its own ranks publicly. The footage, widely shared on social media, shows uniformed men believed to be Somali soldiers surrounding a young man who appears to be in custody. The men are seen placing a plastic bag over the prisoner’s head, apparently suffocating him, triggering widespread condemnation online. The SNAF Command said the investigation would determine the circumstances of the incident and identify those responsible. “The SNAF Command strongly warns all personnel against engaging in such conduct,” the military said in its statement. The statement did not name any soldiers shown in the video, nor did it disclose where or when the incident occurred. It also did not clarify the identity or current condition of the man seen being held. Officials said personnel found to have violated prisoner-of-war protections or broader human rights standards would face both legal and military disciplinary action. “Firm legal and military disciplinary action will be taken against anyone found to have violated the laws of armed conflict, the rights of prisoners of war or human rights,” the statement said. Rights monitors and international law experts have indirectly noted that mistreatment of detainees during counter-insurgency operations can undermine both battlefield legitimacy and cooperation with foreign backers, according to [source/report, if available]. The SNAF has not said whether any soldiers have been arrested or suspended pending the outcome of the investigation. The case comes as Somali government troops and allied fighters continue offensives against Al-Shabaab in multiple regions, part of a broader campaign to reclaim territory from the militant group. items.title: US Court Clears Way to End TPS for Somali Nationals
items.summary: A federal court in Boston has cleared the Trump administration to move forward with ending Temporary Protected Status for Somali nationals, affecting more than 1,000 people in the United States. The post US Court Clears Way to End TPS for Somali Nationals first appeared on Radio Dalsan .
items.body: Federal Court Clears Trump Administration to End TPS for Somali Nationals BOSTON, United States — A federal court in Boston has cleared the administration of President Donald Trump to proceed with its decision to terminate Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Somali nationals, a move affecting about 1,100 people living in the United States. The ruling was issued by Judge Allison D. Burroughs of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts. She granted the government’s request to lift a temporary injunction that had prevented the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from implementing the termination of Somalia’s TPS designation.TPS is a U.S. immigration programme that allows nationals of designated countries facing armed conflict, natural disasters or other extraordinary and temporary conditions to remain legally in the United States and obtain work authorization while the protection remains in effect.Somalia was first designated for TPS in 1991 , amid the country’s civil war. The designation has been extended and redesignated repeatedly over the years because of continuing security and humanitarian concerns. Why is Somalia’s TPS being terminated? In January 2026, DHS, then led by Secretary Kristi Noem, announced that the United States would terminate Somalia’s TPS designation. A notice published in the Federal Register said the decision followed a review of conditions in Somalia and consultations with other U.S. government agencies. The administration concluded that Somalia no longer met the statutory requirements for continued TPS protection. DHS argued that conditions related to the conflict in Somalia had changed significantly since the country was first designated in 1991. The department also cited considerations involving national security, foreign policy, public safety and what it described as problems associated with the U.S. immigration system. The administration further argued that the security situation in Somalia no longer prevented Somali nationals from returning to the country. According to DHS data, 1,082 people held approved TPS status as of December 8, 2025, while another 1,383 applications were pending at the time.The termination was initially scheduled to take effect on March 17, 2026. However, on March 13, a federal court temporarily blocked the move after Somali TPS holders and two immigrant advocacy organizations challenged the government’s decision. The legal challenge The lawsuit was brought by four Somali nationals, along with African Communities Together and the Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans .The plaintiffs argued that the decision to terminate TPS was unlawful and alleged that bias and discriminatory considerations had influenced the administration’s decision-making process.Judge Burroughs had previously paused implementation of the termination while the case proceeded. The legal situation changed significantly, however, after the U.S. Supreme Court issued a ruling on June 25, 2026 , involving TPS protections for nationals of Haiti and Syria. The Supreme Court removed lower-court orders that had temporarily blocked the termination of TPS for Haiti and Syria, giving the Trump administration greater ability to proceed with TPS terminations.Against that backdrop, Burroughs on August 14 granted the government’s request to lift the injunction blocking the termination of Somalia’s TPS designation.The judge acknowledged that the plaintiffs had demonstrated that they could face serious harm if TPS protections were removed. However, she concluded that the Supreme Court’s ruling made it difficult for her to issue the relief they were seeking. What does the decision mean for Somali TPS holders? The termination of TPS does not mean that every affected Somali national will automatically be deported on the day the court ruling was issued.However, people who rely solely on TPS to maintain lawful protection in the United States could lose their protection from removal as well as their employment authorization once the termination takes effect. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) updated its guidance on Somalia’s TPS termination on August 5, noting that the original March 17 termination date had been delayed because of the court order. The American Immigration Lawyers Association (AILA) also reported in 2026 that the final court restriction preventing the termination of Somalia’s TPS had been lifted on August 14, and that USCIS had indicated that employment authorization associated with Somalia’s TPS would end on that date.The underlying legal dispute, however, did not necessarily end with the August 14 ruling. While the judge rejected the plaintiffs’ request for emergency relief and allowed the government to proceed with the termination, other legal arguments raised by the plaintiffs remain part of the broader case. The decision could have significant consequences for Somali nationals in the United States, particularly those who do not have another legal immigration status allowing them to remain and work in the country.The future of Somalia’s TPS designation will depend on the outcome of the continuing litigation and any further legal or administrative action by the U.S. government. The post US Court Clears Way to End TPS for Somali Nationals first appeared on Radio Dalsan .

items.title: DR Congo Ebola cases jump above 6,000
items.summary: Since outbreak declaration in May, virus has killed more than 2,900 people in Congo, according to health authorities
items.body:
Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo surpassed 6,000 on Monday as authorities intensified efforts to contain the outbreak, official data showed.

Congo has reported 6,041 cases, including 2,911 deaths, since the outbreak was declared in mid-May, according to the Health Ministry’s latest situation update.

At least 1,366 people have recovered, while 619 patients remain in isolation or hospital.

The latest Ebola outbreak in Congo is the world’s second-largest by recorded infections, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, has affected 60 health zones across six provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo.

The ministry said response efforts remain concentrated in areas with active transmission, with particular attention to Ituri, which accounts for the majority of cases and affected health zones.

The rise in cases and wider geographic spread over the past three months represent a “substantial increase” in the scale of the outbreak, according to the WHO.

The government has rolled out an Ebola vaccination campaign targeting health and frontline workers.

The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) announced last week a new $16.5 million partnership with African biopharmaceutical company Minapharm Group to develop its Bundibugyo vaccine candidate.

items.title: 200 fighters defect from Sudan's paramilitary RSF, join army: State media
items.summary: Latest defection follows departure of hundreds of fighters, several commanders from paramilitary group in recent weeks
items.body:
A force of 200 fighters has defected from Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and joined the Sudanese army, state media reported Sunday.

The group, which included prominent field commanders, arrived in Omdurman, west of the capital Khartoum, according to the state-run Sudan News Agency.

The force was led by Abu Bakr Hamouda Dahloop, commander of the special missions intelligence division in North Kordofan state, the agency said.

The group announced that it was joining the Sudanese army with all its equipment and was ready to take part in combat operations alongside the military and allied forces.

Dahloop said the fighters had realized "their mistake in following the project being implemented by the RSF militia."

He said they had joined the "national camp" and would fight "for the demands of the Sudanese people to eliminate the rebel RSF militia."

The latest move follows several other reported defections from the RSF in recent weeks.

On Aug. 19, Sudanese authorities announced that four military commanders, 318 fighters and 50 combat vehicles had defected from the RSF.

That group, led by Lt. Col. Musa Ali Ahmed, known as "Khamsin," joined the army, according to authorities.

On Aug. 13, authorities said another RSF force comprising 21 commanders and 270 fighters had defected and joined the army.

The RSF has also seen defections among senior field and political figures, including Fares Al-Nour, political adviser to the RSF commander; Maj. Gen. Al-Nour Ahmed Adam, known as "Al-Nour Al-Qubba"; and field commander Ali Rizqallah, known as "Savanna."

The three Kordofan states -- North, West and South -- have witnessed clashes between the army and the RSF since October 2025.

Sudan has been embroiled in war between the army and the RSF since April 2023. The conflict has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

items.title: Imported From Egypt: The Extremist Ideology That Inspired Boko Haram
items.summary: This is the story of how modern Islamist extremism emerged from the edge of an African prison and moved into Nigeria, escalating into an unending fire of insurgency. The post Imported From Egypt: The Extremist Ideology That Inspired Boko Haram appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: In August 2016, Mamman Nur, one of Boko Haram’s foremost commanders , dramatically sat before a camera on the shore of the Sambisa Forest, a vast terrorist hideout in North East Nigeria. He publicly accused the group’s supreme leader, Abubakar Shekau, of doctrinal deviance and transgressions. He said Abubakar had become power-drunk, killing his own commanders over minor disagreements and spilling the blood of fellow Muslims. He named several terrorist figures Shekau had killed, including Mustapha Chad, Abu Amr Falluja, Kaka Allai and Mallam Ba’ana Banki. He titled the recording Exposé , deliberately weaponising the same word Shekau had used to attack his critics. He also invoked the words of the former Islamic State spokesman Abu Muhammad al-Adnani , saying: “Whoever changes, we will also change him.” His message was not only a threat; it was also a campaign to depose Shekau as the leader of the terror group. Within months, Mamman’s faction formally broke away to become the Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), as Shekau led the Jama’atu Ahlussunnah Lidda’awati wal Jihad (JAS). This movement had existed before Boko Haram pledged allegiance to the Islamic State. Behind the sudden division lay an unfolding theological debate within the global Salafi-jihadi movements for decades. It revolved around one question that has repeatedly divided jihadist organisations from the Middle East to the Lake Chad Basin: How far can the practice of takfir – declaring other Muslims as non-believers – go before this doctrine, which is meant to validate jihad, starts to undermine the very concept of jihad itself? Drawing on Boko Haram’s internal correspondence, Arabic treatises, multimedia recordings, and local sermons, HumAngle traces how an ideology born in Egypt travelled through Jordan, Iraq, and Syria before taking root in northeastern Nigeria. What later appeared as a personal power struggle between Shekau and Mamman Nur was, in reality, the culmination of a decades-long ideological dispute over faith, authority, governance, and the limits of violence. The journey that turned the former terrorist allies into bitter enemies began several decades back, in an Egyptian prison cell. Sayyid Qutb: Reinventing the concept of jahiliyya A popular photo of Sayyid Qutb while in detention in Egypt. Source: ABC News The story begins with Sayyid Qutb, an Egyptian author and one of the foremost figures in modern Sunni Islamic revivalism. He’s the author of a popular Islamist book, Ma’alim fi al-Tariq, mostly known as Milestones , which he wrote while in prison under the Egyptian President Gamal Abdel Nasser, and published shortly before his execution in 1966. The book was said to have transformed a classical Islamic concept into a revolutionary political doctrine. The term “jahiliyya” literally referred to the pre-Islamic Arabian era before the Prophet Muhammad’s message, but Sayyid gave it a radically different meaning in his book. He argued that contemporary Muslim societies had fallen back into a new jahiliyya because they accepted political systems that placed human authority above divine law. Sayyid firmly believes that sovereignty is solely God’s domain. He argues that any government that creates laws outside of Sharia, even if its leaders identify as Muslims, is essentially practising a modern form of paganism. The solution, he claimed, was the emergence of a committed Islamic leadership capable of separating itself from corrupt society before working to transform it. That radical framework would become one of the most influential ideas in contemporary jihadist literature. Variations of it would later appear in the writings and speeches of militant organisations from Egypt and Jordan to Iraq, Syria, and Nigeria. The book’s influence on Boko Haram was neither indirect nor accidental. Mohammed Yusuf, Boko Haram’s founder, openly defended Sayyid against critics within Nigeria’s Salafi movement. In one of the sermons reproduced in The Boko Haram Reader, a book edited by Abdulbasit Kassim and Michael Nwankpa, Yusuf warned his followers against reading books that dismissed Sayyid and Hasan al-Banna , the founder of the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational Sunni Islamist organisation founded in Egypt in 1928. He praised Sayyid as a scholar whom Allah had granted a unique understanding of communism and what he described as polytheistic political systems. Citing the Albanian-born Syrian Hadith scholar Muhammad Nasir al-Din al-Albani , he argued that no contemporary scholar had explained the meaning of la ilaha illa Allah (there is no god but Allah) as comprehensively as Sayyid had in his book, Milestones. He also claimed that Sayyid’s writings played a role in inspiring Osama bin Laden. Throughout much of his public preaching, the Boko Haram founder portrayed himself as someone restoring the original teachings of Islam rather than introducing new doctrines. However, his sermons revealed that one of the intellectual foundations of his terrorist organisation had been laid decades earlier by an Egyptian author, who had written from prison. Although Sayyid didn’t create Boko Haram, he introduced the conceptual language that jihadist ideologues expanded, refined, and eventually transported into northeastern Nigeria. From diagnosis to doctrine Abu Muhammad Al-Maqdisi, a Salafi-Jihadi ideologue who is the key intellectual of modern jihadism. Source: Wikipedia While Sayyid seemed to have established the groundwork for radical jihadist ideologies, Abu Muhammad al-Maqdisi, a Palestinian writer and Salafi Islamist , developed the legal framework. Born in 1959, the Jordanian ideologue emerged during the 1980s as one of the most influential theorists of modern Salafi-jihadism. His book Millat Ibrahim (The Religion of Abraham), completed in 1984, built on Sayyid’s concepts of sovereignty, transforming them into a practical doctrine. Abu Muhammad argued that leaders who chose to govern by conventional, secular laws, instead of divine revelation, have deviated from the teachings of Islam, and therefore have abandoned the religion. From this, he developed the concept of takfir al-hukkam (declaring such rulers as apostates) and the doctrine of al-wala’ wal-bara’ (complete loyalty to believers and total disavowal of unbelievers, their institutions, and political systems). In his publication with the Combating Terrorism Centre , Joas Wagemakers, an associate professor of Islamic and Arabic Studies at Utrecht University, stated that Abu Muhammad was the first prominent Islamist to publicly declare the Saudi ruling family apostate for embracing the idea of democracy. His influence spread far beyond his own extremist writings. In the mid-1990s, he met a young Jordanian militant named Ahmad Fadil al-Khalayleh, better known as Abu Mus’ab al-Zarqawi , in prison. The two spent years together in detention, with Abu Muhammad serving as Abu Musab’s principal ideological mentor. When Abu Musab later established al-Qaeda in Iraq after the U.S. invasion of 2003, he carried much of that intellectual framework with him. The relationship eventually became the first major case study of a pattern that would later recur within Boko Haram. Abu Mus’ab Al-Zarqawi. Source: The Guardian By 2004, Abu Mus’ab had taken the excommunication doctrine far beyond what his teacher considered acceptable. His campaign against Iraqi Shiites relied on mass excommunication and indiscriminate violence, treating entire communities as legitimate military targets. Abu Muhammad publicly objected to his approach. After his release from prison in July 2005, he told Al Jazeera that it was “forbidden to equate the ordinary Shiite with the Americans in warfare”. His objection was not over the legitimacy of jihad itself but over the widening circle of Muslims being declared unbelievers. Abu Mus’ab rejected the criticism, claiming his mentor’s intervention harmed the jihad in Iraq instead of resolving it. The dispute would soon draw the attention of al-Qaeda’s top leaders. In July 2005, Ayman al-Zawahiri, then Osama bin Laden’s deputy, sent Abu Mus’ab a letter that has since become one of the movement’s most important internal documents. Ayman warned that the indiscriminate killing of Shiite civilians was alienating ordinary Muslims and undermining al-Qaeda’s broader objectives. He questioned why Iraqi Shiites should be targeted wholesale when many could be excused because of ignorance. This theological qualification would later reappear almost verbatim in Boko Haram’s own internal correspondence. The disagreement established a pattern that resurfaced repeatedly over the next decades. First, an ideologue developed the doctrine. Then a militant commander applied the doctrine more aggressively than its authors. Finally, an internal rebellion argued that the doctrine itself had been pushed beyond its limits. Years later, Boko Haram replayed almost the same sequence. How the ideology moved to Maiduguri Muhammad Yusuf during a pre

items.title: Algeria sends 4 fighter jets to Niger after unrest in Niamey
items.summary: 2 patrols comprising 4 Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft land at Niamey airport, accompanied by aerial refueling plane, says Defense Ministry
items.body:
Algeria sent four fighter jets to Niger on Sunday following recent unrest in the capital Niamey, the Defense Ministry said.

The ministry said two patrols comprising four Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft landed at Niamey airport, accompanied by an aerial refueling plane.

The aircraft were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities on “a mission to support the Nigerien army in confronting an attempt to destabilize the brotherly state of Niger,” it added.

The deployment was ordered by Algerian Army Chief of Staff Said Chengriha under instructions from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune to strengthen strategic cooperation between Algeria and Niger, “particularly in the military field.”

The ministry said the operation “reaffirms Algeria’s firm commitment and determination to continue its efforts to strengthen security and stability in the region.”

It also renewed Algeria’s “constant support for the government and people of Niger in overcoming this sensitive period.”

Nigerien Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine received the Algerian mission and expressed “his thanks and gratitude” to Tebboune and the Algerian people for the support, according to the statement.

The recent unrest included attacks around Diori Hamani International Airport and Air Base 101, a strategic military facility in Niamey, as well as other sites in the capital.

Niger's defense minister said military activity in the capital Niamey had been brought under control and security forces had regained control of critical sites that were targeted.

items.title: 7 civilians killed, several missing in rebel attack in DR Congo
items.summary: Suspected ADF rebels also set fire to residential houses, says local official
items.body:
At least seven civilians were killed in a weekend attack by suspected Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) rebels in a village in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, a local official said on Sunday.

The attack took place in the Mambasa territory of Ituri province on Saturday, according to Alberic Kahundirwa, a local official.

“The death toll remains provisional because several people are missing. But the attackers also set fire to about 20 houses,” Kahundirwa told reporters.

The latest attack came a week after separate other attacks in various villages in the same territory left 16 people were killed and several others abducted.

The ADF is affiliated with the ISIS (Daesh) and has been active in eastern Congo for several years.

The rebel group is accused of killing more than 1,000 civilians in Congo in 2025, and remains among the most dangerous armed groups in the eastern part of the country, according to a report of UN experts in July.

Noting that the ADF maintained ideological ties and communications with Daesh, the UN experts said systematic and large-scale attacks against the civilian population took the form of killings, abductions and sexual violence, particularly affecting women and children.

items.title: The Scholarly Rebuttal of Boko Haram’s Logic of Terror
items.summary: Different insurgent groups in Nigeria take Islamic texts out of their historical theological contexts to justify their acts of violence and bloodshed. The post The Scholarly Rebuttal of Boko Haram’s Logic of Terror appeared first on HumAngle .
items.body: In his small study at the entrance of his home in Kano, North West Nigeria , Tijjani Ismaila, the deputy imam of the Kwankwasiyya City Mosque, lays out a theological problem that has occupied generations of Islamic scholarship even before Boko Haram’s emergence in northeastern Nigeria. The question is simple yet intriguing: how should verses revealed in one historical era be used to judge situations in a different era that bears little resemblance to the one in which they were revealed? The Islamic cleric emphasises the importance of this question, given the thousands who have died and the escalating armed violence in Nigeria, as extremists impose their interpretations of verses to justify violence whenever and wherever they desire. “They take Qur’anic verses out of context,” he says. “They turn a verse revealed for an active battlefield in seventh-century Arabia into a permanent command even in times of peace. They also misapply a verse about combatant non-Muslims onto a fellow Muslim, because they redefine who is Muslim and who is not according to their own criteria.” For more than a decade, violent extremist groups, most prominently Boko Haram, have manipulated Islamic texts to justify their terror campaigns, stripping theological principles of their historical or logical contexts. Boko Haram and other jihadist organisations in Nigeria rely on three theological theories . One is hakimiyya , which brands any government not run on its version of Sharia as illegitimate; another is jihad – interpreted as permanent war on whom they regard as nonbelievers – and takfir , a concept allowing the group to declare fellow Muslims disbelievers and legitimate targets. Insurgent groups rely on these fundamental concepts to legitimise civilian massacres, abductions, and forced labour. The Kano-based Islamic scholar presents a counter-narrative that addresses the three concepts and critiques the classical scholarship that extremists rely on. Sheikh Tijjani Ismaila Khalifa, the deputy imam at Kwankwasiyya City mosque. Credit: Aliyu/HumAngle. Hakimiyya: “Rulership belongs to none but Allah” The jihadists’ foundational claim is that any government not run strictly on its version of Sharia is illegitimate, and that Muslims who serve it, vote in it, or simply live peacefully under it have committed kufr, an act of disbelief. There are major disagreements among the jihadists themselves. The Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) and Jama’atu Ahlussunnah Liddaawati Wal Jihad (JAS) split over whether someone living under this secular government without knowing should be excused on grounds of ignorance. But they both agree on the core point that living under the government, or serving in it intentionally, is an act of kufr . The hakimiyya governance system was popularised in the twentieth century by the Indian Islamist ideologue Abul A’ala Al-Maududi. It was later sharpened by the Egyptian Islamist ideologue Sayyid Qutb , who argued that any society not governed purely by Sharia was living in the pre-Islamic period. Sayyid relied heavily on the verdicts of 13th-century jurist and theologian Ibn Taymiyyah, especially on divine sovereignty. However, he applied these ideas in a political and revolutionary context that the medieval scholar never intended. The jihadists’ argument for the radical hakimiyya system rests on Quran 5:44: “And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed; then it is those who are the disbelievers.” Speaking on the Islamic exegesis of the Quranic verse above, Tijjani noted how many people have wrongly interpreted “what Allah has revealed” to mean Sharia law. “When people hear Sharia, the first thing that comes to their mind is criminal law and Hudud (prescribed punishments) such as penalties for theft or alcohol consumption. But Sharia encompasses far more than just penalties. It covers leadership, governance, justice, and ethics,” he said. Comparing modern democracy, the scholar explains that “when you look at modern democracy, there is nothing in its core mechanisms that inherently contradicts Islamic principles. The only point of debate is the source of legislation: whether laws are derived solely from Islamic text or through legislative bodies.” “But even in Islamic tradition, scholars perform Ijtihad (independent reasoning) to formulate rulings where texts are not explicit. Qur’anic texts provide a constitutional framework rather than a minute code for every single societal rule. Therefore, when legislators pass laws that align with public interest and do not contradict explicit Qur’anic prohibitions, this functions similarly to ijtihad,” he says, asserting that the Second Caliph, Umar ibn Khattab, was willing to adapt rulings to new circumstances through ijtihad, demonstrating that Islamic law is designed for flexibility rather than the rigid literalism demanded by jihadist preachers. “There is nothing in [democracy’s] core mechanisms that inherently contradicts Islamic principles.” He adds that Islamic governance has never required a rigid theocracy in the way jihadist groups imagine. The constitution of Medina – the Prophet’s own charter for governing a mixed community of Muslims, Jews and pagan tribes – was, in his description, a civic document built for coexistence, not a template for excommunicating everyone outside one interpretation. The cleric explains that the verse the jihadists quote has a far narrower classical reading. Ibn Abbas, one of the earliest interpreters of the Quran, was asked directly what it meant, and explained it means “disbelief less than disbelief”. He clarifies that mainstream commentary from early scholars asserts that the verse’s most severe judgment is directed at the rejection of the law’s divine origin, rather than at every administrative failure to implement it. “Their problem stems from their fundamental way of thinking. They follow only the surface level of the text – what is called literalism. They look at a verse literally without considering its actual meaning or context of revelation. They drew these ideas from certain perspectives, such as their reading of Ibn Taymiyyah, who attempted to dismiss metaphor (majaz) and insisted that words in the Qur’an or Hadith must be taken strictly as they appear,” the Islamic scholar adds. Jihad and the sword verse The second pillar is Quran 9:5, often called “the verse of the sword,” which instructs Muslim believers to fight polytheists after a grace period expires, “wherever you find them”. The jihadists also quote a hadith in which the Prophet says he has been “commanded to fight people until they testify there is no god but Allah.” Extremists in the Sahel have deployed these texts to recruit naive individuals into what they term open-ended war against unbelievers. Responding to this, Tijjani stresses that the extremists have only taken a single text in isolation to justify their radical beliefs, ignoring complementary texts and the overall objectives (Maqasid) of Islamic law. “Historically, the Prophet, peace be upon him, lived peacefully alongside non-Muslim neighbours and communities,” he said. “Any Hadith or verse regarding fighting must be contextualised within the broader framework of the Qur’an. Allah says: Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. The Hadith [that says] I have been commanded to fight the people… cannot mean fighting every human being on earth simply for not being Muslim, because Islam explicitly forbids forcing people into religion. Faith requires genuine conviction.” But there is another problem. Jihadists claim that every verse of the Quran that promotes peace was abrogated after the religion became powerful and Muslims constituted the majority of people in Medina. However, Tijjani disputed that claim, calling it a popular but weak argument. “The claim that peace verses were completely abrogated is largely an issue of scholarly interpretation (Ijtihad), not an explicit textual declaration from the Qur’an itself. Verses regarding peace, diplomacy, and coexistence remain valid and applicable depending on the circumstances and context of the Muslim community. The idea that all peaceful interactions were permanently cancelled is a misunderstanding used by extremists to justify perpetual conflict,” he says, noting that some scholars within the Hanafi School of Jurisprudence rejected abrogation altogether and tied verses strictly to their historical occasion. Scholars who accepted abrogation never read the 9:5 verse as a license to kill any non-Muslim anywhere; the dispute inside the tradition was about which boundary applied, not whether the verse had one. The cleric pointed to the Prophet’s record of honouring peace treaties like the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah, which was kept even when his companions thought its terms were unfavourable. “Islam’s default state in international relations and human interaction is peace,” he says, reiterating that war in the classical framework is a defensive, e

items.title: US welcomes Obasanjo’s Tigray visit as fears of renewed conflict grow
items.summary: The US embassy in Ethiopia says it has been encouraged by former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo’s visit to Mekelle yesterday. In a statement, US Ambassador Ervin Massinga said Mr Obasanjo’s work under his African Union mandate was critical at a time of mounting concern over renewed fighting. Tensions between the Tigrayan authorities and Ethiopia’s federal government have remained high for mo
items.body: The US embassy in Ethiopia says it has been encouraged by former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo’s visit to Mekelle yesterday. In a statement, US Ambassador Ervin Massinga said Mr Obasanjo’s work under his African Union mandate was critical at a time of mounting concern over renewed fighting. Tensions between the Tigrayan authorities and Ethiopia’s federal government have remained high for months, fuelling fears that the conflict could once again erupt into war. Mr Massinga said all sides should instead focus on addressing the drought conditions affecting communities across the country, as millions of people across the region face acute hunger. The Greater Horn of Africa is enduring one of its worst droughts in decades, compounded by years of conflict and instability and the effects of a strengthening El Niño event. “Getting people home and back to their productive lives, safely and with dignity, should be the objective of all leaders, and that will take compromise,” he said. “We look forward to engaging former President Obasanjo on this matter of critical importance to the future of the people of Ethiopia,” Mr Massing added. However, TPLF leaders say Mr Obasanjo’s visit to Mekelle “produced no new proposals or tangible progress towards dialogue with the Ethiopian federal government.” In a statement issued today, the TPLF said Mr Obasanjo’s visit was made without a prior appointment, but that Tigray’s president rearranged his schedule to meet him. During the meeting, the TPLF “expressed disappointment over what it described as a lack of meaningful follow-up to discussions held in June, when several issues were identified as potential entry points for dialogue” with the federal government. The post US welcomes Obasanjo’s Tigray visit as fears of renewed conflict grow appeared first on Ethiopia Observer .

items.title: At least Six Dead in Addis Traffic Accident
items.summary: ADDIS ABABA – A traffic accident involving a minbus and an excavator claimed the lives of at least six people in Addis Ababa on Monday, according to a
items.body: ADDIS ABABA – A traffic accident involving a minbus and an excavator claimed the lives of at least six people in Addis Ababa on Monday, according to a police report. The deadly accident occurred in the morning of August 24 when a bucket of the excavator fell on a moving minibus taxi in Bole Subcity of Ethiopia’s capital. Six passengers were killed in the accident, the Addis Ababa Police said in a statement issued Monday. The driver and several other passengers aboard the minibus also sustained serious or minor injuries. They were taken to nearby health facilities for medical treatment, said the Police, who have launched an investigation to determine the exact cause of the accident. The incident is among a series of deadly traffic accidents in the East African nation, which are often linked to reckless driving, weak law enforcement, poor vehicle conditions and other factors. With vehicle numbers rising alongside the country’s growing economy and expanding middle class, experts call for stricter safety enforcement, thorough vehicle inspections, and a more rigorous licensing system to prevent future tragedies. — EM, news agencies

items.title: From Guantanamo Bay to ISCAP: The case of Jamal Kiyemba
items.summary: In 2002, Jamal Kiyemba, a Ugandan national living in the United Kingdom, was arrested in northwest Pakistan after allegedly attempting to join Al Qaeda in Afghanistan and was sent to the US prison facility at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. Released in 2006 and sent to Uganda, Kiyemba has since been in and out of prison, most recently over his support of the Islamic State’s Central Africa Province (ISCAP).

items.body: The last time Aster saw her husband was when he left for work after lunch. As he usually did, he said goodbye to his wife and their two-year-old child before leaving. It would be the last time Aster saw him alive. Later that day, she called her husband several times. He told her that he and his colleagues were safe but warned her not to leave the house because no one knew what might happen. Aster’s fear stemmed from reports that two federal “army commanders” had been killed on Saturday, 21 October 2023. The area was tense. The two commanders were killed outside a small business run by Aster’s husband. Soldiers accused him of informing Fano fighters about the commanders’ movements, leading to their deaths. The 36-year-old, the owner of the business, and a security guard were taken to a temporary military camp for questioning. Only one of the three returned alive. “I waited until about six in the evening. Then I heard gunshots. I was terrified, but I never thought they would kill him. No one deserves to die like that. It’s not just because he was my husband. He was a kind and generous man who treated everyone the same, whether they were family or strangers. He always put others before himself,” Aster said, her voice breaking with emotion. A few hours after he was taken away, Aster’s husband was found dead on the road. Their child was only two years old at the time. Another man who was killed was a security guard whose body was found near the camp; he had previously served in the defence forces and was a father of three:his wife was eight months pregnant. As the conflict in the Amhara region enters its fourth year, civilians continue to bear the cost of the violence. People like Aster’s husband and the security guard, who were not directly involved in the fighting, have paid the ultimate price. ACLED, which monitors political violence and conflict around the world, said that since the start of the Fano insurgency in April 2023, millions of people in the Amhara region have been affected by violence. Between February and August 2026 alone, more than 8 million people were exposed to conflict. According to ACLED, the violence has affected all parts of the Amhara region, with the heaviest fighting reported in West Gojjam, North Wollo and North Shewa. Both government forces and Fano militias have been accused of committing abuses, although government forces have been blamed for the majority of the reported violations. Observers say the government has not only failed to fulfil its legal and moral responsibility to protect the rights and safety of its citizens, but has also become a perpetrator of abuses. The region has been under a state of emergency since August 2023, with restrictions on civil rights still in place. Reports indicate that many attacks targeting civilians take place after clashes between the two sides, while a significant number of residents have also been killed by heavy weapons that missed their targets and struck civilian areas. Beyond the fighting on the front lines, there have also been targeted killings of government officials. Government forces have also targeted families whose members have joined Fano, with reports of relatives being arrested or killed because of their alleged links to the armed group. The killing of local officials . On 6 June 2024, Milishu Bekele, the administrator of Kewet woreda in North Shewa, was killed on the road. She was six months pregnant at the time and was among the government officials killed by insurgents in the Amhara region. Since the outbreak of the conflict, many local officials have been forced to leave their homes and live inside administrative buildings under tight security, according to their family members. Milishu, who had worked in the health sector for 15 years, was killed while on her way to spend the night at the administrative office. Her husband said she was ambushed by two individuals he identified as Fano members. Officials in Oromia and Tigray have also been killed in attacks linked to their association with the government. ACLED’s 2026 report surveys 66 incidents of violence targeting local officials around the country. The Fano armed group more than doubled its attacks on local officials over the past year, targeting both individuals and public institutions and weakening local administrations. Seen by armed groups as representing opposing interests, local officials have borne a heavy toll from the conflict. The group has targeted woreda administrators, cabinet members and Prosperity Party officials. South Gondar Zone appears to have been particularly affected, with several woreda administrators and government officials killed. One source said local officials who speak out strongly against Fano during meetings are particularly likely to be targeted. The source said the group gathers information on local officials, selects those it wants to target, and sends them threatening messages warning that they will be killed. The source said more than 10 local officials he personally knew had been killed in the zone.The threats against government officials have forced many of them to work remotely or from safer locations.Officials can only travel under strict security arrangements and are often forced to spend the night in military camps for their safety. South Gondar police chief Commander Niggus Tamene said assassinations of local officials increased in 2025 and 2026. Human rights reports indicate that government security forces have subjected the families of Fano members and civilians accused of supporting the group to harassment, threats, arrest, property seizures, killings and other abuses. In August 2024, in Dejen town, six-month-pregnant Nitsuh Mekonen, whose husband had been accused of being a Fano member, was taken from a police station along with her mother-in-law. Both women were later killed, according to relatives. Family members said Nitsuh and five other relatives, including children, had been arrested in an attempt to pressure her husband to return. ACLED data show that fighting between the two sides accounted for about 80% of conflict events recorded in the Amhara region over the past three years, highlighting the scale and spread of the violence. More than eight million people have been exposed to conflict. The conflict in the region tends to intensify during military operations and then subside. ACLED senior analyst Jalale Getachew Birru said these operations can trigger a sharp increase in clashes, often lasting for two weeks or even a month, before the fighting declines. He said the clashes are not confined to battlefields but often take place in villages where people live, making the human toll particularly heavy. An excerpt from a longer report published by BBC Amharic. The post The overlooked conflict in the Amhara region appeared first on Ethiopia Observer .

items.body: Fighting between federal forces and rebels from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which lasted for several hours, ended on Saturday, local and security sources told AFP on Sunday. A TPLF member, speaking on condition of anonymity, said armed clashes in Shererina, near the Sudan border, involving heavy artillery and drone strikes, began at about 6:00 am on Saturday and ended around 5:00 pm. The source said the fighting was slowing down but did not provide any information about casualties. On Saturday, the TPLF accused the federal authorities of escalating their military actions and launching what it described as a “large-scale infantry offensive.” Abraham Belay, head of the Ministry of Irrigation and Lowlands, who is originally from Tigray, confirmed that clashes had erupted between federal forces and TPLF fighters. In a Tigrinya-language statement posted on his official social media page, he accused the TPLF of initiating hostilities in the Shererina area and warned that continued fighting could lead to further harm. The clashes came after tensions between the two sides had intensified in recent months, following that TPLF leaders had dismantled the regional interim administration established by the federal government and taken control. The post Fighting ends between federal forces and TPLF, but calm remains fragile appeared first on Ethiopia Observer .

items.title: Calls for greater international attention to Amhara conflict
items.summary: A call was made for the European Union, the United Nations and the wider international community to give greater attention to the ongoing conflict in the Amhara region, the Reporter newspaper reported.
